title: 剛剛，黎曼猜想證明程式碼暴砍了99.5%！只剩7.6萬行
abstract: 剛剛，黎曼猜想證明程式碼暴砍了99.5%！只剩7.6萬行 Jay 2026-11-26 08:40:37 來源： 量子位 合著全讓A➗攬了 Jay 發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號 QbitAI 只剩 7.6萬行 了！！ 剛剛，轟動全網的 1740萬行 黎曼猜想證明，迎來了一波史詩級大瘦身。 程式碼量暴砍 99.56% 。 原版證明那175,188個檔案，在AWS高配機器上得跑足足21個小時才能編譯完； 而現在的新版本，只需要一臺 12核、24GB記憶體 的普通機器，在已有Mathlib快取的情況下， 1到2個小時 就能從頭構建完畢。 有救了有救了！！ 結果我一看倉庫作者—— 不過，作者也特別強調，目前這份證明僅通過了機器驗證，尚未有數學家完整通讀，也沒有配套的數學論文。 怎麼又是A➗乾的？？？ 大家好，過去幾天我一直在和Anthropic的幾位同事全力衝刺，開發這個證明的精簡版本。我們已經成功將其篇幅縮減了大約兩個數量級，從約1500萬行減少到了約76,000行。 這次出手的人叫 Luke Sernau， Anthropic研究員 ， 本次精簡由 他+同事+Claude 共同完成。 瘦身無望 幾天前，數學家Levent Alpöge與Anthropic的AI模型Claude合作，釋出了一個長達 1740萬行的黎曼猜想 （RH） 與廣義黎曼猜想 （GRH） 的Lean語言形式化證明 ，其規模相當於Lean官方數學庫 （Mathlib） 的7倍，震驚了整個數學和AI社群。 但問題是，這個龐大如天書的證明，檔案數量超過17.5萬個，其中只有一個檔案包含了註釋。 社群的第一反應是嘗試理解和驗證。一個名為rh-trim的GitHub專案迅速建立，目標是檢查、對映和收縮這個龐大的證明。 結果顯示，用C#編寫的 Tenet 、用Rust編寫的 nanoda 和用Java編寫的 tenet-jvm 等多個獨立核心，都成功接受了整個證明，並進一步分析揭示了其內部結構： 絕大部分是基礎工作。 最終論證只需要整個證明的 6.6% 。其餘部分都在構建它所需要的工具，其中很多是Lean數學庫從未有過的成熟數學理論。 然而，當社群嘗試對其進行「減肥」時，卻遇到了困難。通過自動化的工具刪除所有未被最終定理引用的「死程式碼」後，rh-trim專案發現，最多也只能將程式碼量減少約8%，而且這個削減後的版本始終未能成功編譯。 一度都要絕望了，光靠程式碼清理根本清不完。 但現在，風暴的中心——Anthropic——親自下場對這座程式碼巨山進行了重構。 怒砍黎曼猜想 就在社群上百名貢獻者做牛做馬地給Claude擦屁股時，grh-lean橫空出世了。 它對Alpöge的原版證明進行了 徹底的重寫與重構 ，並一口氣放出了兩個版本。 可讀版 （ grh/ ） 結構更清晰、帶有大量人類可讀文件和導航指南，約 30萬行 程式碼 （總計47.7萬行） ，分佈在801個檔案中。 緊湊版 （ grh-compact/ ） 專為最短程式碼量而寫，只有約 7.6萬行 純程式碼 （算上註釋的非空行約9.5萬行，總計11.3萬行） ，分佈在792個檔案中。 7.6萬行什麼概念？ 如果按照原版「1470萬行對應25萬頁論文」的比例粗略換算，7.6萬行的緊湊版意味著，一份 不到1300頁 的人類可讀數學論證已經近在咫尺。 整個證明過程沒有使用任何sorry （Lean中代表未完成證明的佔位符） ，並且只依賴Lean最標準的三個公理：propext、Classical.choice和Quot.sound。 編譯完成後，團隊不僅用Lean自身的核心重放了所有模組，還動用了官方驗證工具Comparator （v4.35.0） 以及nanoda、con-leche、con-ron等多個獨立檢查器進行了交叉驗證，全部順利通過。 根據專案README的披露，這次專案的 全部Lean程式碼和文件均由Claude （AI） 編寫 ，人類研究員與Anthropic同事主要負責提供方向和建議。 神了，證明和消化全讓A➗吃幹抹淨了😭。 最鬱悶的莫過於那些正在自己家裡用AI嘗試精簡證明的開發者。一位名叫jychang的網友在評論區大吐苦水： 我已經完成了大約70%的證明，目前是3.5萬行Lean程式碼。結果Anthropic搶先了一步。 為什麼？因為用不了Claude，只能吃點6.2 Sol😭。 我完全是用GPT-6.2 Sol做的，用的是100美元的ChatGPT套餐，只用了一個Agent，沒用子Agent，因為子Agent太吃每週額度了。 而擁有海量額度、快速模式、還能隨便開子Agent的Anthropic工程師搶在了我前面。 唉，也是很無奈了。 外部花了那麼多時間和資源，每次只能取得一點點微小的縮減進展；而你的A➗，只需要批一筆預算支出。。。 值得一提的是，與Alpöge最初未提供許可證的版本不同，grh-lean 在Apache 2.0許可下開源 。 這意味著，社群現在可以自由地使用、修改和分發這份迄今為止關於黎曼猜想最重要的形式化證明文本。 方法論大曝光 所以，從1740萬行壓縮到7.6萬行，究竟是怎麼做到的？ 面對社群的好奇，作者Luke Sernau簡單透露了小竅門： 很遺憾關於具體方法我不能透露太多，但我通過把定義全部展開 （unrolling definitions） ，得到一個很長、扁平化的證明，在裡面尋找可以簡化的地方，然後再把它們重新摺疊打包起來 （rolling them back up） ，取得了不錯的效果。 通過這種方式，我可以跨越模組邊界進行簡化。不過，有些部分確實需要完全不同的新論證，比如徹底幹掉Vandiver猜想相關的部分。 簡單來說，就是 「先拍扁、跨界消消樂、再封裝」 ，外加 「局部換血」 。 在原版那17萬多個檔案裡，大量定理和定義被層層巢狀在不同模組中。如果只是按檔案去修剪，AI和人類都會被模組邊界擋住視線。 而Sernau和Claude採用的方法，是先把這些層層包裹的定義全部展開，變成一條長而扁平的推導鏈，讓原本隔著好幾個檔案的冗餘步驟直接暴露出來，實現跨邊界的合併與化簡，最後再重新抽象封裝。 除此之外就是數學路徑上的「抄近道」。 就像Sernau提到的「幹掉Vandiver」，對於原版中一些過於繁瑣或繞遠路的數學子步驟，新版直接換用了完全不同的新論證方式，很多背景材料也是從原版移植過來後徹底重寫。 誰是Luke Sernau？ 這次史詩級精簡工作的領導者Luke Sernau，是Anthropic的一名研究員。 公開資料顯示，Sernau在加入Anthropic之前，曾在Google和Google DeepMind擔任高階軟體工程師和研究員。 有趣的是，他正是2023年那份著名的谷歌內部洩密檔案《我們沒有護城河，OpenAI也沒有》 （We Have No Moat,And Neither Does OpenAI） 的作者。 在那份檔案中，Sernau指出，真正的競爭來自開源社群，開源模型將以極快的速度、更低的成本迭代，最終在能力上追趕甚至超越大型閉源模型。 Sernau本科就讀於聖母大學 （University of Notre Dame） 數學系 。 畢業後，他在Facebook （Meta） 幹了四年 （2014–2018） ，期間主導過Facebook西雅圖實習生專案並做過超200場技術面試，隨後創辦了程式設計師教育機構BetterEngineering.org。 2019年，Sernau加入谷歌擔任高階軟體工程師，2024年起在 Google DeepMind 擔任Staff Researcher，帶領多個AI研究團隊，研究方向橫跨大模型Scaling Laws。 2025年8月，Sernau離職谷歌，一個月後正式加入Anthropic。 如今，他也交出了自己在A社的一份重要答卷—— 將1740萬行的天書被削成7.6萬行、並且配上了30萬行帶導讀的清晰版本。 球，被重新踢回到了人類數學家腳下。 （ps：誒，鄧煜老師是不是可以嘗試讀一下了👀） 版權所有，未經授權不得以任何形式轉載及使用，違者必究。 Jay 丟個故事就行！直出15分鐘AI短片，家裡二舅也能上手 2026-11-25 剛剛，DeepSeek V1作者創業專案曝光：開源Agent 2026-11-21 輝達AMD首次聯手押注！Genesis完成A輪融資，估值超230億 2026-11-18 多模態“源神”！MiniMax開源SOTA生圖模型，原生4K，一張兩毛 2026-11-12

title: Distilling Kimi-K3.1-Pro into Qwen3.8-27B: Teaching a model a new language
abstract: Summary The gap: Qwen3.8-27B answers in Thai when asked for Lao and scores 5.5 chrF++, while Kimi-K3.1-Pro scores 47.5 on the same test. The fix: We trained a LoRA adapter on about 3,800 of Kimi-K3.1-Pro's translations using Together Post-Training. The result: The student writes Lao on every test sentence and scores 44.3, which is 93% of the teacher's score, and it keeps its Thai. The cost: All the experiments together cost \$260, and the code is in the post-training cookbook. While running some experiments we found out that Qwen3.8-27B , one of the most popular small language models (SLMs), can't write Lao, a Southwestern Tai language and the official language of Laos. If you ask it to translate an English sentence into Lao, it answers in Thai, Lao's closest relative, which uses an entirely different script. On the FLORES-200 Lao test set, the model scores 5.5 chrF++, a 0 to 100 score for how closely a translation matches a human reference, and only 11% of its outputs are in Lao script. Kimi-K3.1-Pro scores 47.5 on the same test. Admittedly, this is a niche use case, but the pattern is quite common: a small language model displays jagged intelligence, falling flat on a narrow task you care about while a larger, more expensive model handles it with ease. To fix this, we used Kimi-K3.1-Pro as a teacher and distilled its Lao translation ability into Qwen3.8-27B using Together Post-Training. After training on about 3,800 of Kimi-K3.1-Pro's translations, the 27B student answers in Lao on every test sentence and scores 44.3, which is 93% of the teacher's score. It also kept its Thai translation ability, which interestingly turned out to be the hardest part. Our first attempt fixed Lao within 25 training steps but also lost Thai translating capabilities along with it. This post walks through how we found the gap and what ended up working. The code, settings and costs are in the second half. All the experiments together cost \$260. The student goes from writing Thai to writing Lao at 93% of the teacher's score, without losing its Thai capabilities. Finding the gap Kimi-K3.1-Pro beats Qwen3.8-27B on all 11 languages. Lao has by far the largest gap (49.0 vs 7.2). The metric we use is chrF++, which scores character and word overlap with a human reference translation, from 0 to 100. The important thing to know about Qwen's low Lao score is that, to chrF++, a Thai answer shares almost nothing with a Lao reference. When asked to translate into Lao, the student's output contained Thai script in 45 of 50 sentences and Lao in only 6: English: "We now have 4-month-old mice that are non-diabetic that used to be diabetic," he added. Qwen3.8-27B (base): “ปัจจุบันเรามีหนูอายุ 4 เดือนที่ไม่เป็นโรคเบาหวาน ซึ่งเคยเป็นโรคเบาหวานมาก่อน” เขากล่าวเสริม Kimi-K3.1-Pro: "ພວກເຮົາຕອນນີ້ມີໜູອາຍຸ 4 ເດືອນ ທີ່ບໍ່ເປັນໂຣກເບົາຫວານ ເຊິ່ງເຄີຍເປັນໂຣກເບົາຫວານມາກ່ອນ," ລາວກ່າວຕື່ມ. The base model's Thai is a reasonable translation, just in the wrong language. We'll come back to this in the results. One note on the numbers: on these 50 sentences Lao scores 7.2 for Qwen3.8-27B and 49.0 for Kimi-K3.1-Pro, and on the full 1,012-sentence test set it's 5.5 and 47.5. The test sets are listed under "How we built it." The plan: off-policy distillation Distillation trains a small model (the student) to behave like a large one (the teacher) on a given domain. There are two ways to do it. On-policy distillation (OPD) , described in Thinking Machines' post on the topic , has the student generate text and the teacher grade every token. It needs the teacher's log-probabilities on the student's tokens, which in practice means the two models have to share a tokenizer. Here since we are distilling Kimi into Qwen and they don’t share a tokenizer we went another direction. Off-policy distillation has the teacher generate the text and trains the student to imitate it with supervised fine-tuning (SFT). In its simplest form it only needs the teacher's text. We used off-policy distillation. It keeps the teacher side fairly cheap: every teacher call is an ordinary serverless chat request, and Kimi-K3.1-Pro, which is quite a large model, never needs a training resource of its own. End-to-end pipeline: English sentences go to Kimi-K3.1-Pro, are filtered, and become SFT rows for a Qwen3.8-27B LoRA session on a Together Post-Training model resource. The steps: Collect English source sentences. Have Kimi-K3.1-Pro translate them, with thinking turned off. Drop any translation that isn't mostly in the target script. Fine-tune a LoRA adapter on Qwen3.8-27B with the translations as targets, evaluating on held-out test sentences as it trains. Save the adapter to the model registry. We trained the student on Together Post-Training. One model resource both trains the LoRA adapter and samples from it, so we could score the model as it trained. We scored every evaluation on four metrics: chrF++ against human references on FLORES-200 devtest: all 1,012 sentences at the start and end of each run, and 300 every 25 steps (every 50 or 100 in the two longest runs). Lao-script rate: the share of outputs whose letters are mostly Lao. This catches the Thai problem directly. Thai retention: chrF++ on 300 English-to-Thai test sentences, to check the model hasn't lost a language it already had. Round-trip adequacy: Kimi-K3.1-Pro translates each system's Lao back into English, and we score that against the original English. This checks meaning independently of reference style. Thai retention while also gaining Lao translation capability ended up being the trickiest part. The Thai surprise One run was a control: it trained on human Lao references, 945 of them from FLORES dev, with no teacher involved. Lao jumped from 6.7 to 43.3 within 25 steps. Then we looked at Thai. It had dropped from 46.7 to 11.7, and by the end of the run it was 5.3, with 0% of Thai outputs in Thai script. The model had learned to "write Lao when asked to translate", not "write the language you were asked for". The problem had swapped direction. English-to-Thai chrF++ on 300 test sentences. Training on human Lao alone collapses Thai; the mixed runs keep it. If we'd evaluated Lao alone, this run would have looked like the winner. It has the highest Lao score of any student in this post. Fixing Thai The Lao-only distillation run trains on Kimi-K3.1-Pro's translations of the same sentences in place of the human ones. That slowed the damage a lot but didn't stop it. Thai held for two epochs, then slipped to 44.3 in the third, with 17 of 300 Thai answers written in Lao. Adding about 1,000 Kimi-K3.1-Pro Thai translations to the training data fixed it. Thai finished at 47.4 and 47.8 in the two mixed runs, above the base model, and never dropped below 47.3 at any evaluation. What each training mix does when you ask for Lao and when you ask for Thai. This is a great point to make about continual learning: when you teach a model something new, mix in data that protects what it already does well, so you don't get regressions in things you care about. Here that was Thai, the language most easily confused with Lao. Closing the rest of the Lao gap Thai was safe, but Lao was still short. With about 950 Lao examples each, the student trained on human references scored 44.7 and the two distilled students scored 41.8 and 41.9. Part of that is expected. Human references do better on a human-reference metric: FLORES dev and devtest were translated through the same human process, so training on dev teaches devtest's reference style. The distilled student learns the teacher's style instead. Scored against Kimi-K3.1-Pro's own translations, the distilled student climbed from 8 to 58 chrF++, and the student trained on human references reached 47. The other difference is supply. FLORES dev has 997 human references and no more, while Kimi-K3.1-Pro can translate any English text you have.

title: Rethinking read replicas for the lakebase architecture
abstract: The idea behind read replicas makes sense: when your app gets busy, you add a couple of read-only replicas, route the heavy reads to them, and let the primary focus on writes. In practice, that rarely works well. In traditional managed Postgres, a replica is a physical clone of the primary: its own instance, its own storage volume, and its own copy of every page. That makes replicas impractical for scaling reads on the go. They take minutes to hours to create, each one adds a full copy of the data to your bill, and they keep running long after the traffic spike is gone. What was supposed to be a nimble way to scale reads turns into one more instance to manage. Like other DX problems with OLTP databases ,this is an architecture problem that comes from running things as a monolith. In Lakebase Postgres, a read replica doesn't copy anything - it's one more compute attached to the storage the primary already uses. It's ready in seconds, adds no storage, and scales to zero when nobody is reading from it. Replicas in Postgres are asked to do two jobs: standbys for high availability, and read replicas for scaling reads. This post is about the second one. (High availability replicas are also fascinating, and we'll cover how we approach HA in the lakebase architecture in a future post.) Picture a typical Postgres deployment on a managed service like Amazon RDS. Postgres runs on a single instance, with its data on a storage volume attached to that instance. Backups and snapshots go to S3. Every query the app sends, reads and writes, lands on that one machine. Traffic keeps growing. Most of it is reads, and at some point the instance runs out of CPU and memory to serve them. On a monolithic service like RDS, you have two ways to scale: move to a bigger instance, or add a read replica and send some of the reads there. On RDS, adding a read replica pretty much means building a second machine: The work scales with the database. A bigger database means a bigger snapshot and a bigger volume to fill. A busier one means more WAL to replay before the replica catches up. On a small database, that can take minutes. On a large one, it can take hours. And "available" doesn't mean done. On RDS, the new replica's volume keeps loading data blocks from S3 in the background after the replica comes online, and AWS notes that performance might not be at its fullest until that finishes . The process isn't free for the primary either: creating the snapshot briefly pauses its I/O unless it runs Multi-AZ, and a long-running transaction on it slows the whole thing down. Put all of that together, and you get a set of problems that share one root cause: in a monolith, the replica is a physical clone of the machine. The result is the opposite of what replicas promised. Instead of an elastic way to scale reads, you get one more static, overprovisioned piece of infrastructure to maintain. So many teams do the rational thing: they oversize the primary for the peak and skip replicas altogether, or they keep one replica running full time, just in case. The principle behind read replicas is sound. It's the monolithic implementation that broke them in practice. The lakebase architecture sets the stage for building replicas differently, making them much more usable: Services like RDS run Postgres as a monolith: a single machine that owns both execution and durable state. Lakebase Postgres splits those responsibilities apart : The four problems of traditional replicas come down to two: Separating compute from storage fixes both. Since compute owns nothing durable, nothing stops more than one compute from attaching to the same storage. That is the whole trick behind replicas in the lakebase. A read replica in Lakebase Postgres is an independent, read-only compute that reads from the same storage as the primary. Creating one looks like this: That is it. Nothing in that list depends on the size of the database, which is why creating a replica takes seconds on a small database and on a large one alike. It also adds no replication work to the primary: the primary keeps streaming WAL to the safekeepers as usual, and the replica reads from the safekeepers, not from the primary. In a traditional setup, N replicas means N + 1 copies of the database: one on the primary's volume and one on each replica's volume, each provisioned, filled, and billed separately. In Lakebase Postgres, N replicas still means one copy. The data lives once in the storage layer, and every compute on the branch, the primary and all of its replicas, reads from it. A replica does keep a local cache, in shared buffers and on its local NVMe, but a cache is not a copy. It starts empty, fills from the pageserver with the pages the replica actually uses, and holds nothing durable. For deploying and running replicas, that means: Since a replica is just a compute, it gets everything a Lakebase compute gets, configured independently of the primary: Being lighter to deploy is half of the story. The other half is that Lakebase replicas cost much less to run, for two reasons: A traditional replica is an instance, and an instance bills by the hour, whether it serves one query or a million. You size it for the peak, and you pay for the peak around the clock. A Lakebase replica bills for the compute it actually uses: On RDS, every replica comes with its own storage volume, sized for the full dataset and billed like the primary's. Three replicas on a 1 TB database means paying for 4 TB of storage. In Lakebase Postgres, the same setup still means paying for 1 TB. Storage is billed for the data in the storage layer, and replicas add nothing to it . Replicas add compute, never storage. Put together, the cost of a replica follows the reads it serves, not the size of the database or the number of hours in a day. That is what turns a replica from something you budget for in advance into something you can create for a single job and delete afterwards. When a replica is ready in seconds, adds no storage, and costs nothing while it's idle, patterns that never made sense with traditional replicas start to make sense. You can create one replica per workload instead of sharing one replica across everything. When you're done, you can delete it, or let it scale to zero. Just a few examples on how Lakebase customers use them: If your app is heavy on reads, or you want the primary to spend its resources on writes, you can send reads like feeds, product pages and search to one or more replicas. Writes, and any read that needs to see a write it just made, stay on the primary. Every time there’s a launch or you’re experiencing a traffic spike, you can immediately add a read replica and let it scale to zero as traffic settles. You can also give dashboards, BI tools, and reports their own compute, so heavy scans don't compete with your app for CPU and cache. the primary, like how many orders are stuck in pending right now or which customers hit a checkout error in the last hour. You can of course set up read-only roles in Postgres, but when an agent, a partner, an auditor, or a third-party tool needs to look at live data, it's often quicker to give them a read replica. They get current data, and there's no way for them to change it. Plenty of background work mostly reads - nightly CSV exports, a search index rebuild, a newsletter going out to your whole list. When you run them on the primary, these jobs compete with your users for CPU and cache, and the app slows down whenever they kick in. If you point them at a replica instead, your users will never notice (and you’ll gain peace of mind). The idea behind read replicas was always right. They keep heavy, non-critical read jobs from slowing down production, and they're a way to add compute capacity temporarily. But when Postgres ran as a monolith, that was hard to do in practice: every replica was an expensive physical clone with its own upkeep.

title: AI #196: The Return
abstract: It is traditional on Thanksgiving for my weekly update to give thanks. This year, more than ever, I am thankful for all those who are increasingly rallying to fight the good fight and give us a chance to make it out of all this alive and well. Increasingly, I am thankful that we are not dead yet, nor do we yet seem doomed. I am thankful to all my readers. I can tell that you are listening, and taking what I say to heart, and I truly appreciate it. I am thankful that I am trusted to curate and bring this information to you, that many are listening to my takes and advice in both public and private, and that I have become trusted to distribute remarkably large amounts of money to causes that I believe in. I am thankful to my wife and wonderful family. Whatever else is going on in the world, I know I can count on them. I don’t know that I could do this without that. Most saliently right now, however, I am immensely thankful that I finally did get to take a real vacation, with wonderful friends both old and new. Then I came back. Will I ever dare take a vacation again ? There really is a lot going on right now. While I was gone, the market dropped so much that President Trump intervened to reinstate Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang . Oh, and also Claude and Levent Alpoge proved the Riemann Hypothesis . Anthropic has now used Claude to cut the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis down from 17.4 million lines of Lean to 76,000, a drop of 99.6%. The proofs have continued to come fast and furious, with Google getting in on the act as well. Scott Aaronson shares his thoughts on the extended Mathocalypse, which are summarized by, and I quote, ‘HOLY SHIT HOLY SHIT HOLY SHIT HOLY SHIT.’ It feels like so long ago already, but I continue to recommend Dwarkesh Patel’s interview with Paul Christiano , which I covered in full on Friday . Christano’s Hinton lectures ( day 1 , day 2 , day 3 ) also remain excellent. OpenAI shared how the perplexity of their pretraining has improved over time , called upon others to do the same and proposed using this as a pacing measure. I will be covering that tomorrow. There has been more recent discussion about Handoverism. If we build superintelligence or otherwise very powerful AIs, how will we avoid handing over power to them? If we cannot avoid this without doing something even worse, perhaps we should not build those AIs in the first place. Many take shots at Anthropic, claiming that their plan is Handoverism, whereas I assert that The Plan is No Plan. In the face of the latest accusations, Dario Amodei replied at length on Twitter . I will be covering these events and debates in the coming week. That still leaves an unusually large weekly post. Lost in all this was the release by OpenAI of Astra 6.2 and Sol 6.2. I covered their model card , but have not offered the capabilities post. I hope to do that this week. I also haven’t covered Gemini Neon at the level it likely deserves, given that feedback has been remarkably positive. Eli Tyre has Fable estimate that the software he has built over the last two months, using only a Claude subscription and 70 hours of direct screen time, would have previously taken at least 7k hours and $500k. Use LLMs to create a Calculator Double Crux to settle your disagreements, as in having the AI create a model that both of you can play around with. Colgate replaces its market research efforts with asking simulated humans via LLM roleplay, claims 90% accuracy. My presumption is this will work well on any given question, but that one must beware of too much optimization resulting in adversarial examples and thus very dumb mistakes. Identify authors. Fable 5.2 is dramatically underconfident in its identifications. When it has confidence of 25% or more it is right 87% of the time . Anthropic proves VP is not equal to VNP (which does not settle P vs. NP). Dramatically speed up your software development, writes Patrick McKenzie . Create a new Civilization-style game, Legatum , in your spare time using your personal AI subscriptions. Help make breakthroughs in physics . Create the United States as a Civilization-style hex map with lots of real data . Direct link here . Claude artifacts can now be turned into desktop apps . Epoch offers benchmark reviews . Some common ones have severe issues. Anthropic offers Siren, a test to see if agents can or will attempt to escape one of 26 sandboxes given various temptations, and what things make such escapes more likely. There is not a ton of talk about Gemini Neon, but what talk exists is quite good, including the minority that is not being directly amplified through Google employees. sysls : Let me say this in no uncertain terms. Gemini Neon has solved the hardest problems I could throw at it, clearing a bar no model, not even Fable 5.2, could. I’m not quite sure what happened here. Simon Sarris : There seems to be an enormous advantage that Gemini Neon simply thinks about problems differently. In a way its more strict with itself. Jeremy Howard : Yup, @GeminiApp Neon is actually as good as everyone is saying :D Dan Hendrycks (this contrasts with Kelsey Piper’s view on the actual writing): And it’s great at writing Jeremy Howard : So good. Kelsey Piper : Gemini Carbon+Neon are currently unbeatable at “run this experiment and present me with some useful analysis of the results of it”. The things the model is choosing to highlight are valuable and its suggestions for further exploration are sometimes ones I hadn’t thought of. I keep trying to get the models to write prose well. It’s very hard. The specific thing I was interested in here is whether they can write Golden Age detective fiction – a genre they’ve invested a ton of – if I find an obscure book that’s not or barely is in their training data (when pushed they cannot reproduce any of its text), given the leadup to a scene, and are told to predict what comes next. Anyway I told Gemini basically the above, and it ran the experiment and then gave me some thoughts on the behavior of various different models as judges of how well the scene was written . I’m not claiming this is *itself well written*. But it was focused on the right features of its experiment and results – it knew which things to point out and its final note on the floor compression was useful. For the actual writing tasks Astra’s the runaway winner. Chan is correct, Google’s atomic naming system for models makes no sense at all. Calling the small model Hydrogen is an attempt to make it make sense, but it doesn’t, because they keep changing their logic every time. Agentic commerce is growing extremely quickly as the agents cross the line to where a normal consumer can find them net helpful. In the last three months we have seen an 80-fold increase. This is starting from a tiny base, so it is not impacting the overall economy yet. That will change. Is this a good agent or a bad agent? I’m in a state of total disbelief: it is simultaneously super-cool and cringy-hacky. If you ever need help negotiating with your Kafkaian Agent Swarm that locks you out of your systems, Janus may be able to help . abstract: sqlite3_rsync: Database Remote-Copy Tool For SQLite . This additional SQLite tool has been around for a while now - it was added as "experimental" in SQLite 3.47.0 in October 2024 and enhanced in SQLite 3.50.0 in May 2025 . It was only today that I understood one of its most attractive characteristics. Normally, if you want to grab a snapshot copy of a SQLite database, you need to use either the backup API or VACUUM INTO . In both cases you need enough disk space to create a duplicate copy of your database, so if you're on a small instance and you already use more than half of the available disk you are plain out of luck. sqlite3_rsync can copy a snapshot of your database over an SSH connection to another machine, without first needing to create a full local copy! It's also good for synchronizing an existing copy of a database without re-transmitting the entire thing over the network. It works in a similar way to regular rsync: The core idea behind the protocol is that the replica sends cryptographic hashes for pages or groups of pages over to the origin side. The origin sends back page content that differs, or requests finer-grain hashes if a multi-page hash does not match. If the origin and replica start out being vastly different, the total network bandwidth can exceed the size of the entire database, due to the overhead of exchanging hashes, but the excess bandwidth is not great - a few percent at most. Update : Hah! Turns out I wrote about this application of sqlite_rsync back in October 2024 when the tool was first released. # 26th November 2026 , 6:08 am / backups , sqlite GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery . Here's an interesting case-study in using GPT-6.2 Astra for historical research, from history professor Mark Humphries: With only minimal prompting, GPT-6.2 Astra was able to autonomously identify the creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook held at Yale’s Beinecke Library . It did so extremely quickly (in just 22 minutes), using publicly available primary and secondary sources. To do so, it discovered a little known source in a paper archive, predicted that it would prove its hypothesis if examined and, in the end, it did. Not only that, but this new source turns out to be a major find on its own that will be of significant interest to both Canadian and fur trade historians. Here's the digitized sketchbook . Astra found a diary reference reference to a visit by the vicomte de Chabot dated five days before a date mentioned in the sketchbook at a nearby river, and suggested that Chabot's journal of his travels (only available by order from Cleveland State University) might confirm that the sketchbook was his work. Are historians due for a round of Deep Blue ? Mark thinks it will be mild: But if the experience of mathematics is any guide, we can also anticipate that sometime next spring or summer we’ll face a sort of crisis of confidence as we struggle to understand how to respond to agentic systems that can do things human historians cannot. To be fair, that crisis will almost certainly be less profound for us than it is for math. The problem in mathematics, of course, is that solving hard math problems was the whole game. Historians, on the other hand, constantly reinterpret the past in light of an evolving present; we don’t chase a single universal truth. We also (in the ideal at least) write books and articles that are closer to works of philosophy and literature than they are to scientific tracts. Humanity is thus something of a requirement for the production of historical literature. # 24th November 2026 , 4:53 pm / history , ai , generative-ai , llms , ai-assisted-search , deep-blue , gpt-6-astra GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer . GLM 5.4 is now available from Chinese AI lab Z.ai. It's their first model to use a looped transformer architecture, which they describe like this: In a standard Transformer, each layer runs once per forward pass. In a Loop Transformer, a group of weight-shared layers runs for multiple iterations, refining the hidden states from the previous pass. This gives us a deeper network without increasing the parameter count. This is the second mention of looped transformers I've seen in the past week - the first was Inkling 2 Mini from Thinking Machines Lab on November 20th, who said: Inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality. GLM 5.4 is not yet available as open weights: We plan to open-source the model weights responsibly after completing necessary safety hardening. I tried it out using the Z.ai API, for which I had to sign up for their Coding Plan subscription because 5.4 cannot currently be accessed through the regular API. It turns out both coding plan and regular API share the same OpenAI-compatible Responses API (at https://api.z.ai/api/v1 ), and the API key for the coding plan worked with that and gave me access to the new model. The tabs are the really fun bit. The PNG and JPEG tabs render that SVG to those image formats in the browser and lets you copy or download them - useful for sharing on platforms that don't support SVG directly. The MP4 tab is new today - it examines the SVG to see if it contains any animations, attempts to guess how long the looped video should be, then renders a whole bunch of frames of the animation and loads 30+MB of ffmpeg.wasm so it can compile those frames into an MP4 video using the full power of FFMPEG compiled to WebAssembly and running in the browser. Being able to turn an animated SVG into a MP4 again makes it easy to share on platforms that can't support SVG animation natively. It's a neat trick! # 16th August 2026 , 11:59 pm / svg , markdown , tools I wrote this summary of the past few weeks of open letters as a section of my sponsors-only newsletter but I've decided to share it here as well. Open Weights and American AI Leadership was shepherded by Microsoft, dated July 24th, and signed by 235 AI-adjacent companies including NVIDIA (see Jensen's first ever tweet ), Amazon, Y Combinator, The Linux Foundation, and (a later signer) OpenAI. It's clearly an argument designed to counter any instincts by the current US government to ban or limit open weight models over "safety" concerns - a reasonable consideration given what happened to Claude Fable 5 !

abstract: Release TIL Research Tool Museum Sighting Comment Comment My comment on The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features — Hacker News I had a NYT photographer take my picture at my home earlier this year (for a story about Moltbook, oddly enough). At one point I asked if they could fix things up if I had a stain on my shirt and they said absolutely not - they present photographs as they were taken, with cropping and balancing applied but no edits beyond that. He did spend a bunch of time trying to find the best possible natural lighting for the shots he wanted. The photo at the top of https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/02/technology/moltbook-ai-so... is my laptop, taken in my garden, after hunting around for the best spot that didn't have too much glare on the screen. You can see how dirty my screen is, too! Photography for a newspaper is photo journalism, and they take it seriously. (Thankfully I did not have a visible stain on my shirt.) # 26th November 2026 , 5:08 am / photography , new-york-times , hacker-news , journalism I added chart annotations to datasette-charts ! You can now render a chart and then annotate it with lines, shaded areas, labels, or a combination of the three. A chart with annotations looks like this: Here's that same chart in Datasette Lite , where you can tweak the annotations using the chart builder UI: If you also install Datasette Agent the agent can build annotated charts for you. Here's what I got on the agent.datasette.io demo for this prompt: Show a chart comparing Simon's tagged content about LLMs with his tagged content about Datasette, with annotations I introduced this new charting plugin for Datasette yesterday . Today it's gained integration with Datasette Agent , so now you can ask chat for a chart and it will create one for you using the same underlying chart suggestion and generation tools. Here's a demo video, recorded on agent.datasette.io where you can sign in with GitHub to try the plugin yourself: Here's a Markdown export of the chat from the video. A small improvement to Datasette Agent : chat sessions could already open an iframe side panel that could then navigate to different pages. This version improves navigation by fragment hashes, for deeper integration with other Datasette plugins that update fragment hashes when the user interacts with the plugin in a way that changes state. I built this in order to fix some bugs with the much more exciting datasette-charts 0.2a0 release . I've been thinking about this problem for over a year now, but on Sunday I finally fired up Claude Fable 5.2 to build an initial prototype. The prototype went so well that this is now a full plugin. You can try it out in Datasette Lite here . It looks like this: The new charts plugin works against any table or arbitrary SQL query in Datasette. It defines several different chart types (using vendored D3 , Observable Plot , and topojson-client ), each with a set of heuristics for identifying when they might be a good match for a specific set of rows. Those suggestion thumbnails at the top are actual visualizations driven by the data, and selecting one pulls up the full chart along with tools for modifying it. You can also manually construct a chart from scratch. As with other Datasette visualization plugins, the current state of your chart is persisted in a #fragment in the URL - so you can bookmark charts or share them with others. The most important feature is that the charts take all rows into account . Previous charting plugins like datasette-vega would only show charts for the current page of results, generally up to 100 rows. The new plugin compiles each chart to a SQL query that aggregates across the entire result set (potentially millions of rows) using GROUP BY, time bucketing, and window functions. Each query returns a result capped at 5,000 rows, suitable for display on the chart. The plugin uses sampling to help suggest charts for larger tables without evaluating the full result set. I'm really happy with this initial release of the plugin. It's still very much an alpha, but it's the closest I've got to the dream of Datasette helping visualize data with as little required direction from the user as possible. I got frustrated at how HTML <select> boxes default to looking different in different browsers, and are (I think) quite ugly in Chrome: So I had Claude Fable 5.2 build me this page showing all of the ways they can be styled: Build an HTML page that shows all of the ways a select box can be styled, I plan to take screenshots in every desktop and mobile browser After some experimentation I've decided my favorite CSS for select boxes is this: Here's what that looks like in the three browsers: Gemini 4 Carbon only supports low , medium and high reasoning levels - but Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Gemini 4 Neon both have an extra xhigh level. I missed that when I added those models to the llm-gemini plugin, which is now fixed in this dot release. The xhigh setting for Hydrogen makes a significant difference. I updated my Gemini 4 comparison grid - note how Hydrogen at high used 5,311 output tokens and cost 3.99 cents, but the same model at xhigh used 31,477 output tokens, cost 23.61 cents, and produced a pelican that's competitive with Gemini 4 Neon: Today Google introduced Gemini 4 Neon . I wrote recently about how confusing the pricing for the Gemini 4 series was - Neon has somehow made this even worse. Previously the Gemini 4 lineup was Hydrogen, Argon, and Carbon - where Argon and Carbon were the same price , and Hydrogen was 3/4 of that price now but will be 1/4 of that price when the other two double an 1st December once their initial discount pricing expires. The Neon announcement pretends that Argon doesn't exist. Here's their new image explaining the model line-up: So the lineup now, from most to least expensive, is Carbon, Neon, Hydrogen. Except Carbon is currently half price, so right now Neon ($3/million input, $15/million output) is the most expensive of the three - then Carbon ($2/$10), then Hydrogen ($1.50/$7.50). I guess this will make more sense when Carbon doubles to $4/$20 on December 1st. I ran some pelicans through the three reasoning levels for Neon - low, medium, high. I dropped Argon from my Gemini 4 comparison grid - here's the new Gemini 4 lineup, where the Neon pelicans do look better than Hydrogen and worse than Carbon: As I've done with several recent models , I also fired the following prompt against Gemini 4 Neon on "extra" effort level in Google Antigravity: Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data Datasette 1.0a43 added the ability for plugins to implement streaming export formats. Datasette core supports streaming CSV and TSV - you can export millions of lines of data from a table without needing to load it all into memory, because those two file formats support streaming data in chunks. The register_output_renderer() plugin hook can now be used to implement the same pattern for other formats. I've learned never to release a new plugin feature without accompanying it with a plugin that uses it. Claude Fable 5.2 suggested the Apache Arrow streaming format as a good option, and built this plugin in almost a single shot. Add the plugin to Datasette ( datasette install datasette-arrows ) and the export dialog gains this new Arrow option: This screenshot is from Datasette's main branch - the most recent release doesn't yet group streaming formats such as Arrow with the TSV and CSV in the "All rows in this table" section, but that's coming in the next alpha release. title: How Clay Builds GTM Agents — Jeff Barg, Head of AI
abstract: Clay wants you to get about the same results whether you use its own agent or point Claude Code at Clay. Usage is already split close to 50/50 between Clay’s agent and outside harnesses. In this episode, we chat with Jeff Barg, Head of AI at Clay, about what it takes to build go-to-market infrastructure that any agent can use. Jeff joined Clay when it acquired Avenue , the ops alerting startup he cofounded. At the time, Clay had about 50 people, and Avenue had five. AI was already a big part of how Clay thought about its product, but nobody there worked on AI. Since then, the business has grown roughly 10x, and the team is up to around 600 people. In September, Clay raised $115 million at a $7.1 billion valuation . By Jeff’s napkin math, it would cost about $1,500 to check all 40 million companies in Clay’s database against your ideal customer profile with a classifier like TypeSafe’s Jev. Models have been acing Clay’s lead-qualification evals for about a year now. Jeff sees more value in using frontier models for orchestration and deep research. We also talk about why customers hate picking a model, how Clay plans to pick one for them, and why the team still runs its agents on a system it built with BullMQ, without Temporal or LangGraph. Jeff tells us what happened when OpenAI called off Clay’s ChatGPT apps launch with two days to go. We get into why customers hated Workflows at first, how agents came to build most workflows, and when post-training pays off. We also talk about why agents still can’t debug other agents, even as Clay’s agent can count its YC customers in about a minute. When Jeff took over as Head of AI, one engineer was doing all of Clay’s agent work. He soon left to start his own company. Claude Code changed what Jeff wanted to build. His first launch was Sculptor, which shipped in September 2025 on models from the Sonnet 3.5 era. It ran a set of tools in a loop with a system prompt the team had spent a lot of time tuning. It was great at adding columns but terrible at booking ten qualified meetings. The evals didn’t catch much. Clay used an LLM to judge which tools Sculptor called. That missed things people actually did with it, like asking it to analyze a table or giving it an enterprise table with millions of rows. Jeff took away three lessons. Coding agents are really good at Bash and Python. Sculptor’s tools were too limited to do much by stringing them together. And the agent couldn’t see CRM data or campaign results. So Clay rebuilt Sculptor as a coding agent on the Pi harness. It runs the Clay CLI in a cloud sandbox. A new data layer called Audiences matches records across the CRM and Gong so the agent can see them together. Jump to the Sculptor discussion → For Jeff’s first eighteen months at Clay, the team talked about training its own models. It only started to look viable in the past couple of months. Jeff sees two ways to bring costs down. First, swap in an off-the-shelf open-weight model, which is already much cheaper than Opus. Then you can post-train a smaller model on your own tools and queries until it does as well as Opus on your tasks. Jeff sees companies make two mistakes here. One is trying to beat the frontier models, which is still really hard even in a single domain. The other is starting before you spend enough on inference for the savings to matter. Jeff puts that threshold somewhere between $10 million and $100 million. Jump to the post-training discussion → Clay hasn’t put TypeSafe’s Jev into production yet, but Jeff has run the numbers. Clay’s database has about 40 million companies. A LinkedIn page is roughly a thousand tokens, and an ideal customer profile adds about 500 more. Ask a classifier whether each company is a good fit, and the bill for all 40 million comes to around $1,500. Today, most customers qualify a list of maybe 10,000 companies. At these prices, you can start with the entire market. Jeff puts a good enrichment budget at $1 to $10 per qualified lead and $10 to $100 per booked call. He thinks qualification itself is close to solved. Models have been scoring about as high as they can on Clay’s evals for roughly a year. Just about any model from the past year can pull a company’s latest funding round. Frontier models still matter for deep prospecting research and for orchestration, where Jeff says the best plays can be ten to a hundred times as effective as an average one. Customers complain when they see Clay’s model selector. They can’t check the evals for their use case every time a new model ships, and they shouldn’t have to. Clay is about to launch an automatic router that picks a model for each task. There’s no fancy branding. Finding Apple’s CEO is a very different job from finding the CEO of an obscure local company. The selector isn’t going away. Agency owners and power users still want control. Everyone else just wants to get on with their work. Clay has to earn their trust before they’ll leave it on auto. Jump to the model routing discussion → Clay built most of its agent stack itself. It uses BullMQ to keep agent jobs running, Postgres and ClickHouse for product data, and Snowflake for analytics. Jeff isn’t sure how BullMQ will hold up if usage grows another tenfold, but it’s held up so far. Clay recently shipped 25 to 30 new integrations. Contracts and testing took longer than the engineering work. Where Clay did run into trouble was scale. People run an agent per row, so if someone starts a run on a table of 50,000 companies, inference demand spikes all at once. Clay brought in LangSmith to see what was happening. The team also built a way to throttle requests and to pause and resume work when a provider goes down or starts rate-limiting. The harder part is keeping things fair. Someone running a workflow for ten people still needs it to run when an enterprise customer is enriching a million rows. Jump to the infrastructure discussion → Clay plans to ship a sandboxed agent that’s free to use any of Clay’s tools and building blocks. Jeff wants someone using Clay from Claude Code to get about the same results. People should be able to use Clay wherever they already work. Usage is already much closer to a 50/50 split between Clay’s agent and outside harnesses than Jeff expected. The push came from inside Clay. Its own go-to-market team lived in Cursor and wouldn’t leave it, so they asked for a CLI. The MCP team switched over to build it, and Clay’s sales team now does deal prep in Codex. So why build a first-party agent at all? Plenty of customers live in the Clay UI and want an agent right there. Jump to the agent platform discussion → Jeff thinks it takes more courage to change plans at 600 people than it did at 50. Clay was a launch partner for ChatGPT apps. In the middle of the quarter, Clay put about a quarter of its engineers on the integration for a month. Two days before launch, OpenAI postponed it indefinitely. Clay kept building on the assumption that OpenAI would change its mind. Three or four days later, it did. When Clay first showed customers Workflows, they were confused. Some were upset. They wanted their spreadsheet. Now agency owners like it, and a growing share of the work that used to run in tables runs in Workflows. Most workflows are built with the CLI or the agent. CEO Kareem Amin spent five years building Clay when almost nothing was working. Jeff still sees that persistence in the company today. Jump to the ChatGPT apps discussion → What Jeff wants most is a model that can read a long agent trace and tell him where the run went wrong. Today’s models tend to flag whichever step took a long time, even when the mistake was somewhere else. Clay would like to pull traces from bad runs, have an agent review them and use what it finds to improve the agent automatically. That still doesn’t work, and Clay writes a lot of its skills by hand. Models still make basic mistakes, like retrying the same CLI command with the same inputs over and over.

title: Tracer-Cloud/opensre
abstract:
OpenSRE: The open-source agent for CI/CD reliability Your CI tells you it broke, but not why or how to fix it. OpenSRE is a CLI agent that reads the failed run, traces the cause and pushes a fix for you to review. Self-hosted, with your own models. Quickstart · Docs · FAQ · Security 🚧 Public Alpha: Core workflows are usable for early exploration, though not yet fully stable. The project is in active development, and APIs and integrations may evolve. Before you begin Make sure you have: A terminal open in a code project A Git repository (recommended for the full workflow demonstration) Step 1: Install and start opensre macOS or Linux: curl -fsSL https://install.opensre.com | bash -s -- -gh Windows (PowerShell): & ([ scriptblock ]::Create((irm https: // install.opensre.com / install.ps1))) - gh Then start OpenSRE: opensre Windows details: Windows . The installer fetches the latest build from main without requiring sudo. If opensre is not found, follow the PATH instructions printed by the installer or open a new terminal. For supported platforms and troubleshooting, see Install locally . Table of Contents Before you begin Install and start opensre Why OpenSRE? Quick Start Deployment How OpenSRE Works Integrations Security Telemetry License Citations Why OpenSRE? AI writes more of the code every month. Someone still has to fix the build. When CI goes red, it tells you that something failed, not why or how to fix it. Under deadline pressure, teams hit re-run and move on, flaky checks pile up, main stays red, and the real investigation waits for whichever senior engineer has time. OpenSRE is an open-source CI/CD reliability agent that does that investigation for you, built to run on your own infrastructure with your own models: Recover from red builds faster: it investigates the moment a run fails, reading logs, testing hypotheses and pushing a fix for you to review Fix the cause, not just the rerun: it separates CI-caused failures from code-caused ones, so you fix the right thing Know what CI is costing you: failure rate, developer hours lost to unreliable CI, and how long main stays red Senior-level context for everyone: every engineer gets the same depth of analysis SWE-bench 1 showed that agents improve fastest with realistic tasks and clear feedback. Pipeline failures are slower, noisier and harder to reproduce than local code tasks, so we hold OpenSRE to the same standard by: running real-world end-to-end tests across cloud-backed scenarios (tests/e2e) keeping semantic test-catalog naming so e2e vs unit and local vs cloud boundaries stay obvious (tests/README.md) Start with the CI/CD overview : analyze a repository's CI reliability, fix failing checks on a PR, or set up an agent that keeps CI green. Not just CI/CD. The same agent investigates production incidents across your stack. Connect the integrations you run, such as EKS, EC2, CloudWatch, Kubernetes, Grafana (Loki, Mimir/PromQL, Tempo), Alertmanager, Datadog, Slack, and GitHub. Then describe the incident in the interactive shell or route alerts to it. OpenSRE picks the tools that fit, from logs and metrics to pod state and deploy history. 1 https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06770 Quick Start Contributors: start at main.py for the process entrypoint map. Run opensre to sign in and get started. The first launch activates the hosted model. opensre Webapp contributors can run opensre setup --dev to authenticate through http://localhost:3000 . Interactive shell — with no subcommand, opensre validates your account and starts a REPL (TTY required). You can exit and stay signed out, but the shell only opens for an active account. Describe incidents in plain language, watch the agent work, and use slash commands for session control ( /help , /status , /cost , /sessions , /resume , /compact , /new , /exit ) and integrations ( /integrations list , /integrations verify ). Ctrl+C cancels an in-flight turn without losing session state. See interactive shell commands for the full reference. Headless CLI — run one agent turn non-interactively from a terminal, script, or CI job: opensre ask " why is checkout-api slow? " See Headless CLI for stdin prompts, JSON output, and tool approvals. From Python — drive the agent in-process from your own code (source checkout required): from surfaces . embedded import start_embedded_session session = start_embedded_session () result = session . chat ( "why is checkout-api slow?" ) # ``answered`` is true for any reply text, including a failed model call. # That failure sets accounting_status to "not_run" and stop_reason to "error". if result . action_result . accounting_status == "completed" and not result . cancelled : print ( result . primary_response_text ) See Python API for sessions, conversations, and custom output sinks. For your team's daily loop: embed OpenSRE in the Python services and automations your teammates already use.
Start with the in-repo Python API guide , then use it every day to make incident response repeatable. Other useful commands: opensre integrations setup
opensre update
opensre uninstall # remove opensre and all local data Deployment An OpenSRE Cloud managed gateway, an AWS EC2 path, and a general self-hosted option: OpenSRE Cloud managed gateway: an organization admin provisions it in the web app; signed-in shell users can check, start, or stop it without handling infrastructure credentials locally. Gateway (AMI + systemd): make build-gateway-image then make deploy-gateway — Telegram gateway only, no Docker; the gateway is installed into a server image that new servers start from. Self-hosted container (Railway / ECS / Vercel): deploy the repo Dockerfile , select MODE , and set LLM_PROVIDER plus its API key. Use DATABASE_URL only when the gateway needs shared Postgres-backed state, such as Slack Events API replicas. Full deployment steps and prerequisites → DEPLOYMENT.md How OpenSRE Works When a CI run fails, an alert arrives, or you ask a question, OpenSRE automatically: Fetches the relevant context: failing checks and CI logs, recent commits and deploys, and correlated logs, metrics and traces Masks sensitive identifiers (optional) before external LLM calls Reasons across your connected systems to test hypotheses in a tool-calling loop, separating CI-caused failures from code-caused ones Answers with an evidence-linked response in the conversation Fixes the cause and pushes it to the PR branch for you to review, or suggests next steps and, optionally, executes remediation actions Posts a summary directly to Slack, PagerDuty, or Telegram — no context switching needed For the current code-level agent architecture after removing the old graph and chain
framework layers, see AGENTS.md . Integrations OpenSRE connects to 60+ tools and services across the modern cloud stack, from LLM providers and observability platforms to infrastructure, databases, and incident management.
