title: bendlang/bend
abstract:
In the post-AGI economy, humans will eventually stop writing and reading code,
but we still need an ambiguity-free language to communicate our intents to the
AIs building the world around us. Bend is that language. With laws , intents can be more precise than natural language. With proofs , we can mechanically verify the AI implemented our prompts correctly.
And with a fast compiler , we can run that code at peak compute. That's Bend - and nothing else. Bend runs FAST Target: be as fast as C on the CPU, as fast as CUDA on the GPU. Status: Thanks to strong types, purity and linearity, Bend compiles to fast executables
as fast as hand-written C (single-core), and even faster (on 10000s cores). The
entire language runs on the GPU, with full memory unification. Bend checks FAST Target: outperform every proof assistant by several OOMs. Status: Bend's compiler is so powerful it can verify mathematical proofs. Usually, this
is slow. Bend is not. It checks, in under a second, files that other projects
would take minutes, making proofs way more practical. Bend is PARALLEL No threads, no locks, no kernels to write. Split the work in two, and Bend
spreads the calls over every core it can find, then joins them back. Below, pow2(20) divides until one task sits on each of 4,096 GPU cores: Bend BLOCKS mistakes - with proof PROBLEM: How can you trust AI code, without reading it? SOLUTION: By forcing your AI to write a correctness proof . Bend introduces LAWS.bend , a file where you declare rules that your app must
not break. Bend's compiler then guarantees that these laws always hold, by
demanding mathematical proof whenever your code is edited. For example,
consider a game with one law: winning is impossible . Here's how it plays out: Law : winning is impossible So far, it works! New feature: "Claude, make the board wrap around" Without LAWS.bend: Laws broken. AI mistake: merged . With LAWS.bend: Laws intact. AI mistake: blocked ! Without LAWS.bend , a bug was merged. With it, the AI had to retry, until no
bugs were left! In this case, it added a wall, but it could have moved the flag,
made the room kill you, or whatever. The only thing it can't do is commit a bug,
because it is mathematically impossible to break laws in LAWS.bend . The
compiler enforces it. Using LAWS.bend is simple. Ask your AI to formalize your app's rules in LAWS.bend . Example: LAW: "the sum of all balances must be zero" LAW: "players can never pass through solid walls" LAW: "list_sort() must always return ascending numbers" LAW: "array_set() may never be called out-of-bounds" LAW: "winning is impossible" (the demo above!) And so on. Anything you can spell can become a law. Ask your AI to run bend PROOF.bend after editing any code. That's it. Rejoice as your app never again breaks or violates your rules. You can also edit LAWS.bend yourself. Here's how it looks: # LAWS.bend law you_cant_win : # "winning is impossible" for moves : List < Game . Move > # any sequence of moves board = Game . replay ( Game . start (), moves ) # replayed from the start { Game . is_won ( board ) == False {} : Bool } # never leads to victory # PROOF.bend def Laws . you_cant_win ( moves ): # ... written by the AI In short, LAWS.bend is AGENTS.md backed by proof . With LAWS.bend , "make no mistakes" becomes enforceable. Skeptical? Edit the demo's code and break the "you can't win" law! Get Started 1. Install: curl -fsSL https://bend-lang.com/install.sh | sh This bend ignores a project's bunfig.toml and .env ; bun bend2/main.ts from a checkout reads them, so check untrusted code with bend . 2. Tell your agent to use Bend: Add this to your AGENTS.md : When using Bend:
- run `bend guide` to learn it
- use `LAWS.bend` to keep important rules
- run `bend PROOF.bend` before committing
- parallelize the code whenever possible Then, just say: "use Bend"! 3. Enjoy bug-free, fast vibe-coded apps! Hints: Ask it to write laws for anything that can't break. Ask it to parallelize anything you want to be fast. Bend is young. If anything goes wrong, ask it to open an issue. <3 Bend works best on the back-end, on Linux or macOS. Examples Syntax == Python + dependent types import Base # Performs effects on the CPU. def main () -> IO ( Unit ): do IO < Unit > : name : String < - IO . try ( String , IO . get_env ( "USER" )) IO . print ( "Hello, " + + name ) Parallelism == divide-and-conquer import Base # Computes 2^d in parallel: a tree of d levels, one leaf per unit. def pow2 ( + d : Nat ) -> U32 : match d : case 0 n : 1 case 1 n + p : a b = pow2 ( p ) pow2 ( p )
      ( a + b : U32 ) # Runs pow2 on the GPU, via `!`. def main () -> IO ( Unit ): result = pow2 !( 20 n ) IO . print ( U32 . show ( result )) Theorems == laws, Proofs == defs import Base # CLAIM: for every nat x, x + 0 equals x. law add_zero : for x : Nat { Nat . add ( x , 0 n ) == x : Nat } # PROOF: induction on `x`, one rewrite (`%`) per step. def add_zero ( x ): match x : case 0 n :
      { == } case 1 n + xp : % add_zero ( xp ) : { 1 n + Nat . add ( xp , 0 n ) == 1 n + _ : Nat }
      { == } References Guide: GUIDE.md , also printed by bend guide . Effects: EFFECTS.md , custom effects in C and JS, and how to build the C that -o x.c emits. Demos: demos/ , apps, servers and proofs, each with its LAWS.bend . Base: base.bend , the base library, also printed by bend base . Paper: BendTT: An Affine Dependent Type Theory . Paper: BendRT: A Parallel Runtime for CPUs and GPUs . Formalization: bendtt.lean , the kernel of --verdict and its proofs, in Lean. Benches: bench/ , every bench used to make the charts above. Formatter: bend-fmt-lsp , a formatting-only Bend 2 language server. Community language server: bend2-lsp , with formatting, diagnostics, and hover. Community workshop: Bend 2 pocket workshop , the checker and JS compiler in one HTML page, with goals and proof tools, phone first. Community Website: https://bend-lang.com Discord: https://discord.bend-lang.com Twitter/X: https://x.com/bendlang Reddit: https://www.reddit.com/r/bendlang/ Issues: https://github.com/bendlang/bend/issues Limitations - Bend 2 is a new language. Bend 1 programs and HVM do not carry over.
- Everything is annotated and nothing is inferred, so code is verbose.
- No type classes, no traits, and no macros beyond compile-time templates.
- Bend has no tactics or proof search; proving theorems takes extra effort.
- Values are affine: closures and arrays cannot be shared.
- Recursion must terminate; `@unsafe` or `def f?(..)` turns the check off.
- Computed matches (`match f(x)`) aren't supported. Must split it manually.
- There is no syntax for if-then-else: a branch is a match on True and False.
- Numbers are Nat, U32 and F32 only: no U64, I64 or F64 (Metal has no f64).
- F32 is axiomatic: nothing about floating point can be proven.
- Strings are linked lists of characters, so text processing is slow.
- Base is small: expect to write helpers other languages ship built in.
- Effects are few: print, env, time, sleep, spawn, channels, files, TCP, UDP.
  UDP buffers fit IPv4's 65,507-byte payload limit.
- No TLS, HTTP library, JSON or regex for now (you can add them as foreigns).
- Targets are C, Metal, CUDA and JavaScript; Lua, Luau and Python are planned.
- The JavaScript target runs on one core and has no graphics or audio.
- Parallelism requires balanced calls. Flexible parallelism will be added later.
- Atomic arrays shared across threads are experimental and need `@unsafe`.
- One GPU per program, one event loop, and no multi-machine execution yet.
- One C file per program: no separate compilation, no incremental builds.
- Compiling to native is slow (clang/CUDA/Metal). For fast development, use JS.
- The compiler is young and has blind spots (unusually slow programs). Report.
- We don't have as many benchmarks as we'd like yet, especially for the checker.
- The compiler (not kernel) is 99% AI-written and not yet fully audited.

title: mastra-ai/mastra
abstract:
Mastra Mastra is a framework for building AI-powered applications and agents with a modern TypeScript stack. It includes everything you need to go from early prototypes to production-ready applications. Mastra integrates with frontend and backend frameworks like React, Next.js, and Node, or you can deploy it anywhere as a standalone server. It's the easiest way to build, tune, and scale reliable AI products. Why Mastra? Purpose-built for TypeScript and designed around established AI patterns, Mastra gives you everything you need to build great AI applications out-of-the-box. Some highlights include: Model routing : Connect to 40+ providers through one standard interface. Use models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, and more. Agents : Build autonomous agents that use LLMs and tools to solve open-ended tasks. Agents reason about goals, decide which tools to use, and iterate internally until the model emits a final answer or an optional stopping condition is met. Workflows : When you need explicit control over execution, use Mastra's graph-based workflow engine to orchestrate complex multi-step processes. Mastra workflows use an intuitive syntax for control flow ( .then() , .branch() , .parallel() ). Human-in-the-loop : Suspend an agent or workflow and await user input or approval before resuming. Mastra uses storage to remember execution state, so you can pause indefinitely and resume where you left off. Context management : Give your agents the right context at the right time. Provide conversation history , retrieve data from your sources (APIs, databases, files), and add human-like memory with Observational Memory so your agents behave coherently. Integrations : Bundle agents and workflows into existing React, Next.js, or Node.js apps, or ship them as standalone endpoints. When building UIs, integrate with agentic libraries like Vercel's AI SDK UI and CopilotKit to bring your AI assistant to life on the web. MCP servers : Author Model Context Protocol servers, exposing agents, tools, and other structured resources via the MCP interface. These can then be accessed by any system or agent that supports the protocol. Production essentials : Shipping reliable agents takes ongoing insight, evaluation, and iteration. With built-in evals and observability , Mastra gives you the tools to observe, measure, and refine continuously. Get started The recommended way to get started with Mastra is by running the command below: npm create mastra@latest Follow the Installation guide for step-by-step setup with the CLI or a manual install. If you're new to AI agents, check out our templates , course , and YouTube videos to start building with Mastra today. Alternative: Use this pre-built prompt to get started Create a new Mastra project. Mastra is a framework for AI applications and agents on a modern TypeScript stack. Before running the command, ask these questions one at a time and wait for each answer unless it was already provided: 1 . Project name? (default: "my-mastra-app") 2 . Provider? (required; options: "openai", "anthropic", "google", "xai")

If the provider isn't supported, ask again and list the supported values.

Run: ` npm create mastra@latest <project-name> -- --llm <provider> ` The command creates a default Mastra project, installs Mastra skills for detected coding assistants, and initializes Git when appropriate.

After creation, enter the project directory and start the dev server: ` npx bgproc start -n <project-name> -w -- npm run dev ` Open Mastra Studio at ` http://localhost:4111 ` . Studio is the interface for building, testing, and managing agents, workflows, and tools.

Also mention that the Mastra model router provides access to thousands of models: https://mastra.ai/models Documentation Visit our official documentation . Build with AI Learn how to make your agent a Mastra expert by following the Build with AI guide . Contributing Looking to contribute? Pull requests are limited to collaborators only. Therefore you can best help by creating high-quality issues with good reproductions and descriptions. Mastra will then verify your report and prioritize it accordingly. If you want to run Mastra or its tests locally, refer to the development documentation Support We have an open community Discord . Come and say hello and let us know if you have any questions or need any help getting things running. It's also super helpful if you leave the project a star here, at the top of the page Licensing This repository uses a dual-license model: Apache License 2.0 : The core framework and the vast majority of this codebase is open source under Apache-2.0. Mastra Enterprise License : Code in any directory named ee/ (e.g., packages/core/src/auth/ee/ ) is source-available under the Mastra Enterprise License. These features require a valid enterprise license for production use but can be freely used for development and testing. See LICENSE.md for the full license mapping and ee/LICENSE for the enterprise license terms. Security We are committed to maintaining the security of this repo and of Mastra as a whole. If you discover a security finding we ask you to please responsibly disclose this to us at security@mastra.ai and we will get back to you.

title: tianma-if/edgeever
abstract: EdgeEver AI-native note-taking app & Evernote/Obsidian alternative. Instant all-platform sync, rich notes (tables, mind maps, diagrams, posters), web clipper & MCP. 100% free on Cloudflare or Docker. 簡體中文 | 繁體中文 | English | Español | Deutsch | Français | 日本語 | Polski | Русский Telegram Group | 🌐 Live Demo | 🗺️ Roadmap | 📱 Clients & Extension | Feature Matrix & Capabilities | 📥 Note Migration EdgeEver is a modern, open-source notes and knowledge base workspace. It preserves the classic, high-efficiency three-pane productivity workflow (Tree View · Note List · Editor) while offering an open data architecture and seamless AI Agent integration for complete ownership and smart productivity. 💡 Serverless & 100% Free Forever EdgeEver can run within Cloudflare's free quotas with no server purchase or VPS maintenance. Users who prefer a VPS, NAS, or home server can deploy the same application with Docker. ⭐ If EdgeEver is useful to you, consider giving it a Star. Your support helps more people discover the project. Why EdgeEver Many users of note-taking apps and personal knowledge bases simply want a reliable, open, and fast personal knowledge base. However, existing mainstream solutions all present tradeoffs: Evernote : Offers the smoothest, most seamless multi-device cloud sync experience. Yet as it evolved into a full-featured commercial suite, ads and add-ons multiplied while system overhead climbed. Meanwhile, free-tier quotas tightened, premium AI subscriptions grew expensive, and it remains difficult to integrate into modern self-hosted and private AI workflows. Obsidian : Open Markdown files, closed-source core. Official Sync requires an ongoing subscription tiered by storage and vault count, while third-party sync (iCloud, WebDAV, Git, etc.) is tedious and conflict-prone; constrained by local-directory file sync and mobile background limits, it struggles to match the seamless, invisible sync of cloud-native note apps (and lacks a full web workspace). Relying on local file scanning causes noticeable cold-start and search lag once notes reach the thousands or plugins pile up; storing attachments alongside notes bloats vaults, slows mobile sync, and leaves orphaned files behind. Combined with an IDE-like UI and plugin-tinkering learning curve, it feels overly heavy for users used to out-of-the-box, capture-anywhere cloud note apps. Joplin : A veteran open-source three-pane note app, yet its UI design and editing experience feel stuck more than a decade in the past, lacking modern polish and fluidity. Fast official sync (Joplin Cloud) requires a paid subscription; free sync via WebDAV or cloud drives relies on file-by-file polling that becomes sluggish on mobile as notes and attachments grow, while self-hosting Joplin Server requires maintaining your own server with no zero-cost serverless option. It also lacks a full browser-based web workspace and native AI Agent capabilities (MCP/ACP). Memos & Stream Notes : Clean and simple, but their social-timeline layouts differ fundamentally from the structured productivity of a classic three-pane workflow. SiYuan & Block-based PKMs : Powerful with self-hosting support, but their UI and interaction feel closer to heavy Obsidian-style PKMs than the intuitive three-pane experience of traditional commercial cloud note apps, and their granular "block-level" architecture also imposes noticeable cognitive overhead for quick daily capture and continuous prose writing. Furthermore, they lack a true zero-cost serverless deployment tier, and multi-device sync relies on paid official subscriptions or paying extra to unlock S3/WebDAV sync features with your own storage. EdgeEver fills this gap : The entire stack is open source, delivering truly seamless, low-latency, instant multi-device cloud sync with full self-hosting freedom. It keeps the three-pane layout you know, stays silky-smooth and lightweight even with 10,000+ notes, and ships native AI agents with zero-cost deployment. Online Demo Demo: https://demo.edgeever.org The public demo resets every day at 3:00 AM (China Standard Time) and restores sample notes. Do not store private content there. All-Platform Clients & Browser Extension Client Downloads The iOS app requires an Apple ID from outside mainland China. Browser Web Clipper Extension Extract clean Markdown from web articles, clip selected text and images, or capture custom webpage regions directly to your self-hosted instance. Deep structured clipping for 20+ platforms: social (X, Xiaohongshu, Instagram, WeChat, Jike, Douban, Threads, Bluesky), dev & reading communities (Zhihu, Reddit, GitHub, V2EX, Hacker News, Medium, Substack), and media/podcasts (Bilibili, YouTube, Xiaoyuzhou). Feature Matrix & Capabilities An all-in-one workspace connecting inspiration capture, deep creation, and knowledge compounding (👉 Explore 20 step-by-step showcases with screenshots ): Module Core Capabilities & Features Writing, Organizing & Search • Immersive Dual-Mode Editor : Resizable 3-pane workspace, instant toggle between rich-text WYSIWYG and Markdown, built-in template gallery, math & chemical formulas, syntax highlighting, persistent outline folding, and revision history • Custom Typography : Customize covers, chapter navigation, prose color palettes, Polaroid image frames, and spacing per notebook or note • Infinite Hierarchy & Millisecond Search : Unlimited-depth folder trees, tags, drag-and-drop sorting, and batch note merging/moving, paired with instant full-text search and historical filters • Desktop Multi-Window & Large Attachments : Multi-window editing and automatic writeback for externally edited files; automatic 50%–90% client-side image compression and chunked streaming up to 1 GiB Multi-Modal Rich Notes & Visuals • AI Multi-Dimensional Tables & Public Forms : Prompt-to-database generation with named views, multi-condition filtering, multi-field sorting, and clickable cell links; publish login-free collection forms in one click • AI Mind Maps & Architecture Diagrams : Interactive mind maps and live Mermaid flowcharts, sequence diagrams, and architecture diagrams with conversational AI generation • AI Infographics : Conversational one-click generation of timelines, comparison matrices, quadrant charts, and structured visual cards • Native Canvas Poster Notes : Built-in canvas-based visual card note type—double-click to edit covers and social visual cards Omni-Channel Capture & Migration • Browser Clipping & 20+ Platform Parsers : Extract clean articles, clip text/image selections, or capture custom webpage regions; purpose-built parsers for Xiaohongshu, X, Instagram, Zhihu, Reddit, GitHub, YouTube, Bilibili, and more • Mobile Share & Desktop Screen Capture : Save photos and articles via the mobile share sheet; capture screen regions directly into notes via a global desktop shortcut • WeChat Chat History Archiving : Import merged WeChat chat transcripts from mobile or desktop in one click, preserving timestamps, quotes, emojis, and media attachments • One-Click Third-Party Migration : Native GUI import for Evernote, Obsidian, Notion, SiYuan, flomo, Joplin, and Markdown folders with full hierarchies and attachments Styled Publishing & Knowledge Sharing • Standalone Knowledge Base Sites : Publish entire notebooks as standalone static websites with folder tree navigation and optional password protection in one click • Single-Note Share Links : Share individual notes with custom slugs, passwords, expiry dates, view counters, collapsible outlines, QR code downloads, and raw Markdown links • Copy as Rich Text : Preserves formatting and images for pasting directly into WeChat, Zhihu, X Articles, Substack, blogs, and other editors • Curated Long-Image & Multi-Format Export : Built-in long-image poster themes and Monogram avatars; export to high-res images, code cards, MD, HTML, or PDF AI & Agent Collaboration • Companion AI Assistant & BYOK : Sidebar AI for summaries, proofreading, translations, and multi-part

title: twentyhq/twenty
abstract:
The #1 Open-Source CRM Website · Documentation · Roadmap · Discord · Figma Why Twenty Twenty gives technical teams the building blocks for a custom CRM that meets complex business needs and quickly adapts as the business evolves. Twenty is the CRM you build, ship, and version like the rest of your stack. Learn more about why we built Twenty Installation Cloud The fastest way to get started. Sign up at twenty.com and spin up a workspace in under a minute, with no infrastructure to manage and always up to date. Build an app Scaffold a new app with the Twenty CLI: npm install -g twenty
twenty app init my-app cd my-app
yarn install Define objects, fields, and views as code: import { defineObject , FieldType } from 'twenty-sdk/define' ; export default defineObject ( { nameSingular : 'deal' , namePlural : 'deals' , labelSingular : 'Deal' , labelPlural : 'Deals' , fields : [ { name : 'name' , label : 'Name' , type : FieldType . title: Fission-AI/OpenSpec
abstract:
The most loved spec framework. Our philosophy: → fluid not rigid
→ iterative not waterfall
→ easy not complex
→ built for brownfield not just greenfield
→ scalable from personal projects to enterprises Follow @0xTab on X for updates · Join the OpenSpec Discord for help and questions. See it in action You: /openspec-explore
AI:  What would you like to explore?
You: I want dark mode but I'm not sure how to do it cleanly.
AI:  Let me look at your styling setup...
     Cleanest path here: CSS variables + a small theme context,
     with system-preference detection. No new dependencies. Scope it?
You: Yes, let's do it.

You: /openspec-propose add-dark-mode
AI:  Created openspec/changes/add-dark-mode/
     ✓ proposal.md — why we're doing this, what's changing
     ✓ specs/       — requirements and scenarios
     ✓ design.md    — technical approach
     ✓ tasks.md     — implementation checklist
     Ready for implementation!

You: /openspec-apply-change
AI:  Implementing tasks...
     ✓ 1.1 Add theme context provider
     ✓ 1.2 Create toggle component
     ✓ 2.1 Add CSS variables
     ✓ 2.2 Wire up localStorage
     All tasks complete!

You: /openspec-archive-change
AI:  Archived to openspec/changes/archive/2025-01-23-add-dark-mode/
     Specs updated. Ready for the next feature. What do the specs actually look like? Plain Markdown — requirements with concrete scenarios, no special syntax to learn. Here's what goes in the specs/ folder created above: ## ADDED Requirements ### Requirement: Theme selection The app SHALL let users switch between light and dark themes,
defaulting to the system preference. #### Scenario: User toggles dark mode - ** WHEN ** the user clicks the theme toggle - ** THEN ** the app switches to dark mode and persists the choice Your AI writes these; you review the plan before any code is written. OpenSpec is built with OpenSpec — browse this repo's live specs and in-flight changes for real examples at scale. OpenSpec Dashboard Why teams adopt OpenSpec Solo, OpenSpec keeps you and your AI honest on a single repo. On a team, the hard part moves: a feature spans the API server, the web app, and a shared library; requirements are owned by one team and consumed by others; planning starts before any code exists. Stores are the answer — planning in a repo of its own. The same openspec/ shape you already know (specs and changes), shared by git push like anything else. One source of truth your whole team and every coding agent can read, across every repo. Cross-repo features — one change, one plan, even when the code lands in three repos. Shared requirements — a platform team owns the specs; product teams reference them read-only, right where their coding agent can read them. No drifting wiki. Plan before code — capture the plan in the store now; the code repos catch up later. Stores are in beta . Start with the Stores guide . Quick Start Install OpenSpec. On macOS or Linux, in your terminal: curl -fsSL https://openspec.dev/cli/install.sh | sh On Windows, in PowerShell: irm https: // openspec.dev / cli / install.ps1 | iex Prefer a package manager? npm install -g @fission-ai/openspec@latest (needs Node.js 22.20.0 or higher) or the official Homebrew formula , brew install openspec . Then navigate to your project directory and initialize: cd your-project
openspec init Want your AI to do it? Paste the setup prompt into your coding assistant — it installs the CLI, runs openspec init , and verifies the result. Now talk to your AI: Not sure what to build yet? Start with /openspec-explore , a no-stakes thinking partner that reads your code, weighs options, and shapes a plan before any code gets written. ( Quickstart ) Already know what you want? Go straight to /openspec-propose <what-you-want-to-build> . Both are in the default profile. If you want the expanded workflow ( openspec-new-change , openspec-continue-change , openspec-ff-change , openspec-verify-change , openspec-bulk-archive-change , openspec-onboard ), select it with openspec config profile and apply with openspec update . These are skills. Most tools invoke them as /openspec-propose and Codex as $openspec-propose , or you can ask for the work in plain words. openspec init prints the right form for the tools you picked — see Supported Tools . Coming from 1.x and its /opsx:* commands? See Upgrade to 2.0 . Note Not sure if your tool is supported? View the full list – we support 30+ tools and growing. Also works with npm, Homebrew, pnpm, yarn, bun, and Nix. See installation options . Docs Full documentation lives at openspec.dev/docs . → Quickstart : your first change, start to finish → Set up your project : what openspec init installs → CLI : terminal reference → Supported Tools : tool integrations & install paths → Customize : profiles, project config, and schemas → Stores : plan in a separate repo, shared across your team (beta) → Community Showcase : projects and resources built with and for OpenSpec Community schemas Third-party schema bundles distributed via standalone repositories — these provide opinionated workflows that integrate OpenSpec with other tools, similar to how github/spec-kit's community extension catalog handles tool integrations. → Browse the catalog in the customization docs. Why OpenSpec? AI coding assistants are powerful but unpredictable when requirements live only in chat history. OpenSpec adds a lightweight spec layer so you agree on what to build before any code is written. Agree before you build — human and AI align on specs before code gets written Stay organized — each change gets its own folder with proposal, specs, design, and tasks Work fluidly — update any artifact anytime, no rigid phase gates Use your tools — works with 30+ AI assistants via skills How we compare vs. Spec Kit (GitHub) — Thorough but heavyweight. Rigid phase gates, lots of Markdown, Python setup. OpenSpec is lighter and lets you iterate freely. vs. Kiro (AWS) — Powerful but you're locked into their IDE and limited to Claude models. OpenSpec works with the tools you already use. vs. nothing — AI coding without specs means vague prompts and unpredictable results. OpenSpec brings predictability without the ceremony. Updating OpenSpec Upgrade the CLI With the standalone install, run openspec install . If you installed with npm: npm install -g @fission-ai/openspec@latest If you installed OpenSpec with Homebrew: brew upgrade openspec Refresh agent instructions Run this once to refresh the skills installed on your machine. If your team keeps skills in Git, run it in each project that commits them. openspec update Usage Notes Model selection : OpenSpec works best with high-reasoning models. We recommend Codex 5.5 and Opus 4.7 for both planning and implementation. Context hygiene : OpenSpec benefits from a clean context window. Clear your context before starting implementation and maintain good context hygiene throughout your session. Contributing Every change starts as an issue. We discuss it there, and if we agree to pursue it, a maintainer implements the change or invites you to build it with us. → CONTRIBUTING.md : the full process, from first issue to merged PR Other Telemetry OpenSpec collects anonymous usage stats. We collect only command names and version to understand usage patterns. No arguments, paths, content, or PII. Automatically disabled in CI. Opt-out (any one is enough): openspec config set telemetry.enabled false (global config; unset means on) export OPENSPEC_TELEMETRY=0 or export DO_NOT_TRACK=1 (env overrides config) Maintainers & Advisors See MAINTAINERS.md for the list of core maintainers and advisors who help guide the project. title: earendil-works/pi
abstract:
New issues and PRs from new contributors are auto-closed by default. Maintainers review auto-closed issues daily. See CONTRIBUTING.md . Pi Pi is a minimal, extensible agent harness that you can make your own. Adapt Pi to your workflows, not the other way around. Customize Pi with extensions , skills , prompt templates , and themes . Bundle them as Pi packages and share via npm or git. Pi ships with powerful defaults but skips features like sub-agents and plan mode. Ask Pi to build what you want, or install a package that does it your way. Use Pi interactively , automate it in print or JSON mode , control it over RPC , or build apps with the Pi TypeScript SDK . See OpenClaw for a real-world integration. Getting started Install the command-line interface: curl -fsSL https://pi.dev/install.sh | sh On Windows: powershell -c " irm https://pi.dev/install.ps1 | iex " The installer pins all dependencies and updates Pi with pi update . Alternatively, install directly with npm, which does not pin transitive dependencies: npm install -g --ignore-scripts @earendil-works/pi-coding-agent Pi requires Node.js 22.19 or newer. The macOS, Linux, and Windows installers can install it if needed. Pi does not require dependency lifecycle scripts for a normal npm installation. Start Pi in the directory where you want it to work: cd /path/to/project
pi For a built-in AI provider, run /login inside Pi to connect a subscription or API key. Then give Pi a task. See the documentation for full setup and usage instructions, or visit pi.dev for demos. Run with Nix nix run github:earendil-works/pi/stable stable points at the latest release. Install it with nix profile add github:earendil-works/pi/stable and update with nix profile upgrade pi . Use a release tag such as github:earendil-works/pi/v1.0.0 to pin a version, or github:earendil-works/pi for unreleased changes on main . Nix builds Pi from source. Supports ARM64 and x86-64 on Linux and macOS. Use nix build . or nix run . to build or run your checkout. Nix builds are offline, so the bundled model data comes from a pi.dev model catalog revision pinned in nix/model-catalog.json . At runtime, Pi still overlays newer catalog data from pi.dev as usual. The Nix workflow replaces the pin on main when it no longer matches the checkout, for example after a provider is added or gains a new model type. To refresh it by hand: npm run update:model-catalog-pin Packages This monorepo contains the Pi CLI and its supporting libraries. Package Description @earendil-works/chord Object runtime for apps across processes: contracts, documents, a store, links, plugins with hot reload, HTTP, workers, web and terminal clients @earendil-works/pi-telemetry Vendor-neutral telemetry contracts, reference adapter, conformance tests, and typed schemas @earendil-works/pi-ai Unified multi-provider LLM API (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, etc.) @earendil-works/pi-durable Durable conversation, task, and document runtime @earendil-works/pi-agent-core Agent runtime with tool calling and state management @earendil-works/pi-coding-agent Interactive coding agent CLI @earendil-works/pi-tui Terminal UI library with differential rendering For Slack/chat automation and workflows see earendil-works/pi-chat . Permissions & Containerization Pi does not include a built-in permission system for restricting filesystem, process, network, or credential access. By default, it runs with the permissions of the user and process that launched it. If you need stronger boundaries, containerize or sandbox Pi. See packages/coding-agent/docs/containerization.md for three patterns: Gondolin extension : keep pi and provider auth on the host while routing built-in tools and ! commands into a local Linux micro-VM. Plain Docker : run the whole pi process in a local container for simple isolation. OpenShell : run the whole pi process in a policy-controlled sandbox. Contributing See CONTRIBUTING.md for contribution guidelines and AGENTS.md for project-specific rules (for both humans and agents).  Longer term plans for Pi can also be found in RFCs . Development npm install --ignore-scripts # Install all dependencies without running lifecycle scripts npm run build # Refresh model data, then build all packages npm run build:offline # Rebuild using existing model data without network access npm run check # Lint, format, and type check ./test.sh # Run tests (skips LLM-dependent tests without API keys) ./pi-test.sh # Run pi from sources (can be run from any directory) Using local packages outside the monorepo Build every public package into one coherent local artifact set: npm run pack:packages -- --out .artifacts/pi-packages This refreshes model data before building pi-ai . To avoid network access when
model data is already hydrated, pass --offline-model-data . Then configure an external project to consume one package and resolve all of
its Pi dependencies from the same artifact set. npm is the default: node scripts/use-local-packages.mjs \
  --manifest .artifacts/pi-packages/manifest.json \
  --consumer ../my-project \
  --package @earendil-works/pi-durable \
  --package @earendil-works/pi-agent-core cd ../my-project
npm install --ignore-scripts For a pnpm project, point --consumer at the workspace root: node scripts/use-local-packages.mjs \
  --manifest .artifacts/pi-packages/manifest.json \
  --consumer ../my-project \
  --package @earendil-works/pi-agent-core \
  --package-manager pnpm cd ../my-project
pnpm install --ignore-scripts Repeat --package for each direct dependency. The command updates the
consumer's package.json with content-addressed local file: references. It
writes transitive overrides to package.json for npm or pnpm-workspace.yaml for pnpm. Keep the artifact directory available while installing or updating
the consumer. Re-run both commands after changing Pi source. Building standalone binaries from release source GitHub releases include a versioned source archive covered by the release's SHA256SUMS file. Extract it and run the same build script used for the official standalone binaries: VERSION= " <release-version> " tar -xzf " pi- ${VERSION} -source.tar.gz " cd " pi- ${VERSION} " ./scripts/build-binaries.sh --offline-model-data --platform linux-x64 --out " $PWD /out " The archive includes release model data and native prebuilds. --offline-model-data uses that model data without refreshing provider catalogs. The script installs dependencies and builds the executable with its runtime assets; pass --skip-install if dependencies are already provided. Supply-chain hardening We treat npm dependency changes as reviewed code changes. Direct external dependencies are pinned to exact versions. Internal workspace packages remain version-ranged. .npmrc sets save-exact=true and min-release-age=2 to avoid same-day dependency releases during npm resolution. package-lock.json is the dependency ground truth. Pre-commit blocks accidental lockfile commits unless PI_ALLOW_LOCKFILE_CHANGE=1 is set. npm run check verifies pinned direct deps, native TypeScript import compatibility, and the generated coding-agent install lock. The pi.dev installer installs from packages/coding-agent/install-lock/ , generated from the root lockfile, to pin transitive deps. The npm package does not pin transitive deps. Local release smoke tests and npm publication use the same tarball packer; npm publishes the validated tarballs rather than repacking workspace directories. Local release installs, documented npm installs, and pi update --self use --ignore-scripts where supported. CI installs with npm ci --ignore-scripts , and a scheduled GitHub workflow runs npm audit --omit=dev plus npm audit signatures --omit=dev . Install lock generation has an explicit allowlist for dependency lifecycle scripts; new lifecycle-script deps fail checks until reviewed. Share your OSS coding agent sessions If you use Pi or other coding agents for open source work, please share your sessions.

make dev This handles everything: installs dependencies, builds core components, and launches the app. Available make targets: make dev - Full development setup and launch make build - Production build make test - Run tests and linting make clean - Delete everything and start fresh Manual Commands yarn install
yarn build
yarn dev Building on Windows Run make dev from Git Bash (installed with Git for Windows) — make dispatches its recipes through sh , so a plain cmd.exe won't work. You do not need a "Native Tools Command Prompt for VS 2022". The bundled llama.cpp engine builds with Ninja + clang-cl , and clang-cl locates the MSVC toolchain and Windows SDK on its own. What has to be installed (and on PATH for ninja / clang-cl / cmake ): Visual Studio 2022 Build Tools (MSVC x64 workload + Windows SDK) LLVM (provides clang-cl ) Ninja CMake CUDA Toolkit — only for JAN_ENGINE_VARIANT=cuda12 / cuda13 builds Engine variants are picked with JAN_ENGINE_VARIANT (tokens: cpu , vulkan , metal , cuda12 , cuda13 , hip / rocm , joined by - ), e.g.: make dev JAN_ENGINE_VARIANT=cuda13 "nvcc fatal : Could not open output file ...fattn-...cu.obj.d" during tauri-plugin-llamacpp(build) means the build path crossed Windows' 260-character MAX_PATH limit — nvcc does not honor the long-path opt-in. The build script now detects this and automatically relocates the llama.cpp build tree to a short directory under %LOCALAPPDATA%\jan-engine . If you hit path-length errors anyway, set JAN_ENGINE_BUILD_DIR to a short path (e.g. C:\jb ) or move the checkout closer to the drive root. System Requirements Minimum specs for a decent experience: macOS : 13.6+ (8GB RAM for 3B models, 16GB for 7B, 32GB for 13B) Windows : 10+ with GPU support for NVIDIA/AMD/Intel Arc Linux : Most distributions work, GPU acceleration available For detailed compatibility, check our installation guides . Troubleshooting If things go sideways: Check our troubleshooting docs Copy your error logs and system specs Ask for help in our Discord #🆘|jan-help channel Contributing Contributions welcome. See CONTRIBUTING.md for the full spiel. Note: Please sign your commits so we can verify your contributions. title: 0xPlaygrounds/rig
abstract:
Rig is a Rust library for building applications on large language models.
It also ships rig , a terminal coding agent built on the library that you
extend with Bevy plugins. The coding agent cargo install rig
rig This installs the launcher of the latest release. Each release's guide is on
its tag, such as 0.47.0's guide .
The agent guide on main can be ahead of the
release, and shows how to install main from a checkout. The agent needs Rust
1.97.1 or newer and runs on Linux and macOS. The first rig builds the agent, which takes several minutes, and opens it.
Run /login to sign in or save an API key, or export one such as OPENAI_API_KEY before starting. /model picks a model and /help lists
the commands. rig -p "fix the failing test" answers one prompt and exits. Its tools, commands, sessions, sign-in and terminal view are each a plugin,
so any of them can be turned off, replaced or added to. /reload rebuilds
the agent with your changes and keeps the session. The agent guide covers updating, models, sessions, tools,
settings and scripting. The plugin guide explains the basics of a
plugin and points at working examples of each kind. The library cargo add rig anyhow
cargo add tokio --features macros,rt-multi-thread use rig :: prelude :: * ; use rig :: providers :: openai :: { self , OpenAI } ; # [ tokio :: main ] async fn main ( ) -> anyhow :: Result < ( ) > { // Reads OPENAI_API_KEY. let model = OpenAI :: from_env ( ) ? . completion ( openai :: GPT_6_2_SOL ) ; let agent = AgentBuilder :: new ( model ) . preamble ( "You are a comedian." ) . build ( ) ; let response = agent . prompt ( "Entertain me!" ) . await ? ; println ! ( "{}" , response . output ( ) ) ; Ok ( ( ) ) } Rig puts over 20 model providers and a dozen vector stores behind one
interface. It has agents with tools, streaming and typed hooks. It covers
completion, embedding, transcription, audio and image models and follows the
OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions. rig-core and rig-agent build for browser
WASM. See examples/ , the guides and the API reference . Crates The rig crate re-exports rig-core . Its default features add rig-agent ,
the derive macros, the reqwest HTTP client with rustls and, on native targets,
the rig launcher (feature cli , from rig-cli ); default-features = false leaves them out. Each crate in the list below is a feature named after it
without rig- : cargo add rig --features memory,fastembed Agents and state: rig-agent , rig-memory (saved conversations), rig-cassette (record and replay), rig-rmcp (MCP tools). Models: rig-bedrock , rig-vertexai , rig-gemini-grpc , rig-candle (local models), rig-fastembed (local embeddings), rig-typesafeai (TypeSafe Jev judgments). The vector stores, such as LanceDB, Qdrant and PostgreSQL, are companion
crates behind features too; docs.rs lists every feature . Internals: rig-core (messages, models, tools,
providers), rig-derive (feature derive ), rig-http (transport traits), rig-reqwest (feature reqwest ) and rig-tungstenite (feature websocket ). Coding agent: rig-cli (feature cli , the library of the rig binary)
and, not facade features, rig-harness , rig-harness-protocol , rig-ecs , rig-tools , rig-markdown , and the plugins rig-basics , rig-tui , rig-fold , rig-steel , rig-mcp-client , rig-acp , rig-inspect , rig-traffic , rig-bridge and rig-watch . Community Ask questions on Discord . CONTRIBUTING.md says how to contribute, and awesome-rig lists projects
built on Rig. Rig is pre-1.0, so releases break APIs. The changelog and migration notes say what changed. Rig is MIT licensed.

title: AI made self-hosting fun again
abstract:
I’ve been self-hosting things for many years. There were times when I was quite enthusiastic about it, constantly trying out new software and tinkering with my infrastructure. But at some point, that enthusiasm faded a bit. I never really stopped self-hosting, but I became less inclined to experiment with new things. Maintaining what I already had running was enough for me. Over the last few months, however, I’ve found myself getting increasingly excited about self-hosting again. And, somewhat ironically, AI is a big reason for that. Less friction Most of my infrastructure configuration lives in Git repositories, mainly in the form of Docker Compose files, scripts, and other configuration files. This makes it possible to use AI coding agents to work on my infrastructure in much the same way as they would work on any other software project. Whenever I want to try a new service, adjust an existing configuration, or automate something, I can now do so with considerably less effort. In the past, I would sometimes put off certain changes simply because I didn’t feel like spending an evening reading changelogs and documentation or troubleshooting issues. It’s not that I couldn’t have done these things before. But often, the amount of effort required just wasn’t worth it to me. Now, even relatively spontaneous ideas often end up becoming reality. Trying things I always found interesting There are also technologies that I’ve always found interesting but never felt knowledgeable enough about to really make use of them. NixOS is a good example. I’ve always liked the idea of declaratively configuring an entire system; I even used it on my laptop during my Linux honeymoon phase. But getting everything configured the way I wanted was quite a hurdle. With the help of AI, I’m now making much more extensive use of NixOS on my home server. For my VPS infrastructure, I’ve also started building my own Debian-based bootc image (after thinking about it for some time). Having my entire operating system configuration defined in a Git repository and automatically building a bootable container image from it is something I find really cool. But it’s also something I probably wouldn’t have invested enough time in to get working on my own before. Even with the help of AI, it still took me half a day when I set it up a few months ago. Without AI, it would probably have taken me at least a week. AI makes experimenting with unfamiliar technologies much more approachable. I don’t necessarily need to understand every little detail before I can get started. I can learn about things along the way, ask questions, and gradually improve my configurations. Automating almost everything Something I’ve also finally managed to do is automate most of the build, update, and deployment processes for my infrastructure. A lot of the work involved in self-hosting isn’t particularly exciting. Keeping track of new releases, updating container image tags, building images, and deploying configuration changes are all things that need to be done regularly. I still remember what updating a service used to look like: bumping the version and adjusting the Docker Compose file on my laptop, pushing the changes to the Git remote, SSHing into the server, pulling the changes, and finally deploying them. Now, a single Git push is enough. If a push is even necessary. With Renovate, I no longer need to actively keep track of most software updates. It creates pull requests for me, and often, all I need to do is review and merge them. I can even do that on my phone while sitting on the sofa. Pushing changes or merging a pull request triggers the corresponding GitHub Actions or Forgejo Actions workflows, which take care of building and deploying everything. Of course, there’s nothing particularly groundbreaking about any of this. DevOps has been around for a long time, and none of these automation tools require AI. But AI has helped me put all these pieces together in a way that I previously never quite got around to doing. And the nice thing about automating these tasks is that the benefits extend well beyond the initial setup. I now have less tedious work to do every time I want to change something or update a service. Back to more powerful hardware As I’ve started hosting more things again, I’ve also moved more of my services from my VPS to my home server. For a while, I was using an HP t640 thin client as my home server. However, with more things I wanted to run, I decided to switch back to my ASRock DeskMini A300, which had been sitting unused for some time. I’m thinking about repurposing the t640 as a “router on a stick”, though. I even took the opportunity to upgrade its CPU from an AMD Ryzen 5 2400G to a Ryzen 5 PRO 4650G and replaced the stock AMD cooler with a quieter Noctua cooler. Noise was the main reason I switched to the t640 in the first place. It’s nice to put some hardware I already owned back to use rather than buying an entirely new machine. I also managed to get both the CPU and the cooler for a good price through a classifieds site. Having some additional computing power available gives me more room to experiment. And there’s something quite satisfying about having a small box at home running a growing collection of services that I use in my everyday life. Building my own tools But it’s not just about self-hosting existing software. AI has also changed how I approach problems for which there isn’t an existing piece of software that does exactly what I want. Previously, I would often spend quite some time searching for a suitable open-source project, comparing different alternatives, and figuring out how to make one of them work for my particular use case. These days, for smaller problems, building my own solution has become a much more attractive option. I’ve recently built tools to automatically download invoices , e-papers or Linux ISOs . I can build (or have AI build) these tools in Go, my preferred programming language, and tailor them to my exact needs. They don’t need to support every possible use case, have an elaborate user interface, or be particularly interesting to anyone other than me. I don’t need to turn every little tool into a proper open-source project with extensive documentation and support for other people’s use cases. They just need to solve my problem. What I particularly enjoy is how well this complements my increasingly automated infrastructure. Building a small tool has become easier, and so has building a container image for it, deploying it, and keeping it running. The entire process, from having an idea to having something actually running on my home server, requires much less effort than it used to. Just because I can doesn’t mean I should Of course, there are downsides to all of this. Every additional service is another thing that needs to be maintained. AI-generated software isn’t exempt from bugs, security issues, or technical debt. And having an AI agent make changes to my infrastructure doesn’t absolve me of the responsibility of understanding those changes. There’s also the temptation to build or deploy things simply because I can. When implementing an idea becomes so easy, it’s perhaps more important than ever to occasionally ask myself whether it’s actually worth implementing in the first place. On the other hand, self-hosting is a hobby for me. Not everything I do needs to be economically sensible or particularly useful. Sometimes, experimenting with something new is the whole point. And with much of the routine maintenance automated, adding another service doesn’t necessarily mean adding as much recurring work as it used to. A somewhat ironic development? I find it somewhat ironic that AI, a technology largely dominated by big tech companies, is helping me become a little less dependent on those very companies in other areas of my digital life. I’m aware that this also creates a new kind of dependency.

title: AMD-specific fork of llama.cpp
abstract:
tl;dr — I recommend using llama-cpp-rdna-boosts if you have an AMD graphics card. It’s lean, and increased my token generation from 35 to 55 tokens/second, and my prefill from 700 to 1300 tokens per second. YMMV. As of November 2026, an explosion in the number of bespoke inference engines has taken place. Many of them take inspiration from the engines that enabled much of the LLM inference up 'til now: llama.cpp, SGLang, vLLM, etc. The rationale isn’t that those options are bad, but merely that they are generalist engines, optimized for no particular hardware and with a focus on broad compatibility. Others feel the development pace of those engines have slowed down, and with the help of LLMs, they can move faster on their own. Some examples of these new inference engines* are Strata, Basalt, RustingStrata, etc… These new forks generally all have a few things in common: They focus on a specific subset of models and/or hardware They use a frontier model to vibe-code the entire thing They chase ever-higher token generation speeds … and the results are stunning! Strata is able to run a heavily-quantized model of Qwen 3.8 Flash Next, a 180B parameter model , on a 16GB VRAM graphics card, and 16GB system RAM, and have it generate tokens at a surprisingly high rate. In and of itself those three things are not red flags (the second is concerning, of course, but it may be SOP in a year’s time — who knows!), but as these projects have evolved, that relentless chase toward higher token generation speeds has taken an unfortunate turn, in that the optimizations are less about hardware-specific changes, but more about changing how the model thinks so that it goes brrr faster. Strata specifically has taken to preferring to poll experts loaded in VRAM even if other experts (pushed to system RAM/disk) would have been normally chosen. This is just one example, but certainly not the last. That said, I was fortunate to stumble upon yet another project that promised improvements, delivered, and was more aligned with my software development philosophy. Enter llama-cpp-rdna-boosts . It is a repository that contains a minimal set of changes that you apply against a pinned commit of llama.cpp. It is in essence a fork, but one whose changeset is continually re-applied to newer versions of llama.cpp. It contains AMD-specific improvements that drastically improve prefill and token-generation speeds. I appreciate llama.cpp’s approach to software development. They are a stable base to branch off from. Contributions are vetted throughly and applied judiciously. ✅ The rdna-boosts repo is a set of small patches that are applied to base llama.cpp. Fewer moving parts mean fewer things to maintain ✅ The changes are (somewhat opaquely, it’s all straight Claudish 😬) outlined in the documentation, ensuring some degree of transparency. ✅ The setup If you have ROCm libraries installed on your system, you can build the image yourself. I didn’t want to mess with that, so I used the pre-built images published. podman pull ghcr.io/stew675/llama-cpp-rdna-boosts:server-rocm-10.1 This sets up an image that you can run sandboxed via podman to launch the inference server: podman run --rm -it \ --network=host \ --device /dev/kfd \ --device /dev/dri \ --group-add video \ -v "$HOME/models:/models" \ "ghcr.io/stew675/llama-cpp-rdna-boosts:server-rocm-10.1" \ My actual launch script passes a few additional flags, but those are the important lines. I imagine upgrading would be pulling a new image down, though I have not tried this yet. The numbers On my setup, an AMD R9700 connected to my laptop via an eGPU interface, this improved prefill and token generation rates when running ukisai/Swift-1.5-Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF (Q6_K_L) with MTP enabled: Before After Prefill ~700 t/s ~1300 t/s Token Generation ~35 t/s ~55 t/s Strata and its ilk were always promising the moon and it was never clear what steps they took to make that happen. I’m very much looking forward to what the rdna-boosts community come up with next. * It’s worth noting that between these two groups, vllm-radiance made an appearance, which was a fork of vLLM with AMD-specific patches. I tried this too, but the build steps were so onerous and vLLM so overbuilt for my specific use case (1 machine, 1 developer), that I abandoned it and went back to vanilla llama.cpp ← Back to all posts

title: Kamil Khan Mumtaz: Pakistani architect, admired at home, almost invisible abroad
abstract:
Some years ago, my colleague Ben Southwood sent me a handful of grainy online pictures showing some recent buildings in Pakistan. I was struck by the assurance of the designs and the quality of the materials, craftsmanship, and detailing. They seemed to be the work of one Kamil Khan Mumtaz, a Pakistani architect widely admired in his home country but almost invisible abroad. I wondered whether Mumtaz might be the world’s best architect, overlooked because global architecture magazines rarely do photoshoots in Lahore. Last year, I met his assistant Sohaib Ahmed at a conference and immediately entreated him to send Works in Progress any photographs he had of the practice’s work. With Mumtaz’s support, Sohaib prepared a portfolio for us, most of it never before seen outside Pakistan. Image Kamil Khan Mumtaz with a British friend during his studies at the Architectural Association in London in the early 1960s. Kamil Khan Mumtaz was born in Calcutta in 1939 and grew up in what became Pakistan, taking British A-levels at Lahore’s elite Aitchison College. He then moved to London to study at the Architectural Association. Although he had never previously left South Asia, Mumtaz immediately felt at home in England. ‘It seemed completely familiar. I didn’t feel like a stranger at all’, he recalled in an interview with the historian Chris Moffat. ‘I think this is because of having been brought up on essentially English books, in English schools. So, the whole thing was like, “I know this place”.’ Mumtaz enjoyed his studies at the Architectural Association, which taught a standard modernist approach that Mumtaz accepted unquestioningly: ‘I just simply took it hook, line and sinker, and swallowed the whole thing.’ Lahore was one of the capitals of the Mughal Empire, and has a vast endowment of historic architecture and urbanism. Mumtaz prepared a seminal report on its historic core, known as the Walled City. This photograph shows the Walled City during the colonial period. Image Wikimedia . Mumtaz returned to Pakistan in 1966 and began practicing as an architect. At around the same time, he became a communist activist, on account of which he was twice imprisoned by the military dictatorship. He remained resolutely modernist, although he acquired special interest in adapting modernism to the local climate and locally sourced building materials. He also became involved in architectural conservation. In the late 1970s, he prepared a report on the ancient Walled City of Lahore, highlighting its enormous heritage value and arguing for its preservation. ‘Our own bureaucrats only insisted that we should pull down the whole mess anyway, and build new, modern infrastructure and high-rise buildings, et cetera’, Mumtaz remembers. The Walled City was ultimately saved, and parts of it are now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Image Workers’ houses at Kot Karamat, an early Mumtaz project in the late 1960s. They use a local brick, but also feature arched roofs that are alien to rural Pakistani housing. The workers disliked this, preferring flat roofs where they could sleep on summer nights. Through the 1970s, Mumtaz began to question his approach. ‘I had this growing, nagging fear that I wasn’t communicating with my audience, as a visual artist or as an architect. This grew on me, almost like an obsession.’ In 1980, the Iranian architect Nader Ardalan gave him a copy of his book The Sense of Unity: The Sufi Tradition in Persian Architecture . Mumtaz initially paid no attention: ‘Flipping through it, I thought, “Oh yeah, this is traditional Iranian architecture, who cares!” I was totally uninterested.’ But eventually, frustrated by the sense that ‘I didn’t know the language of my own people’, he began to read. ‘From page one, it was mind-blowing. Absolutely. I thought, “My god, what have I been looking for? This is what I’ve been missing!” ... It shattered all of the beliefs I had, being a Marxist, a materialist, an atheist, a modernist.’ In the decades since, Mumtaz has worked to revive the older architectural traditions of Pakistan, and especially of Lahore, his home city. He has built a wide range of buildings, including homes, offices, mosques, and schools. His work has been received with warmth in Pakistan, though also with surprise. ‘I’ve found that there is a huge reservoir of desire, sympathy, and love for our traditional values, forms, architecture, and culture, altogether. But there’s a general kind of impression that these things can’t be done any more, there are no craftsmen who can do this.’ Traditional elements can often be produced in factories, but assembly requires skill even then. Notice how these appliqué columns float slightly above the floor, showing the crudity with which they have been bolted onto the wall. This is from the Quartier Schützenstraße, a Berlin development from the 1990s. Image Author's collection The loss of craft skills is a problem for traditional architecture everywhere. Some elements of traditional architecture have been prefabricated in factories for centuries, but even then, skill is needed for installation. Without skilled craftspeople, important details are often badly executed, making buildings look strange or clumsy. This problem also exists in Pakistan, but its later industrialization meant premodern craft traditions had not quite vanished when Mumtaz began work. Mumtaz recalled that, when searching for skilled craftsmen, ‘immediately, you come into contact with very small remnants of these families, hereditary craftsmen, and so the relationship grows.’ Mumtaz’s work has become steadily more technically sophisticated as he and his craftsmen have built up expertise. ‘Together we have been able to rediscover a number of the practices that had become lost. Certain types of brickwork, the flat dome, the muqarnas [ornamental vaults], many things like this that hadn’t been done. As they tell me, “This has not been done for 300 years!” So, it was a great experience, a voyage of discovery, so much that we learnt from each other.’ It is my great pleasure to introduce our readers to one of the most skilled and thoughtful architects working today. Image An atrium in a private home, before and after plastering. Image A painted dome in a private home. Image Chale Sharif Mosque, Punjab. The brickwork will soon be clad by glazed and patterned tiles. Image The offices of Oxford University Press in Karachi. Image Embossed copper and bronze doors in the Oxford University Press headquarters in Karachi, made by a metalworker Muhammed Hafeez. Hafeez’s ancestors have been specialist metalworkers for generations. Image An open arcade in a private home designed by Mumtaz. Image Courtyards and gardens play a central role in many of Mumtaz’s domestic projects. Image Brick details of Mumtaz’s buildings. Image A carved stone lattice, allowing the flow of air while providing privacy and enclosure. Image Structural brick vaulting over a staircase. Image A covered walkway. Creepers will one day cover the trellis. Image Hand-carved stonework. Image This hall is spanned by four great brick arches, on which nine small brick domes rest. Image The front door of one of Mumtaz’s houses. Image An atrium in a Mumtaz-designed residence. Image Plaster detailing. Image A school for Lahore’s Christian community. This project was built to a tight budget and illustrates the adaptability of Mumtaz’s approach. Image Pak Vigha Mosque in the small town of Kiranwala Syedain in the Punjab. Image The onion profile, tapering point and cord details impart to these marble domes a quality of weightlessness and incipient movement. Image The courtyard of the mosque. Image The arcade is covered by a marble ‘handkerchief dome’. Rather than being terminated by a neat semicircular base, a handkerchief dome wraps around the arches, as though it were a square handkerchief draped over the space it covers. Image Kamil Khan Mumtaz visits a shrine, currently under construction to his designs.

title: YouTube Ad Punisher – Auto-reloads YouTube pages when an ad plays
abstract:
🎯 YouTube Ad Punisher Auto-reloads YouTube pages when an ad plays — preserving your playback position. Punish the ads. The Problem Ad density on YouTube is channel-dependent and changes over time — some channels front-load several ads, others run none. Traditional ad blockers can get detected by YouTube's anti-adblock system ("Ad blockers are not allowed here"), and the skip button takes a few seconds to appear. You sit there, hostage. The Solution Reload the page. That's it. Two reloads and the ad is gone. Every time. 🎯 YouTube Ad Punisher automates this: the moment an ad appears, it captures your exact playback timestamp, reloads the page, and YouTube auto-seeks back to where you were. No ads. No waiting. No skip button hunting. Tips Auto escape: after 3 reloads, the extension automatically switches to a helper tab for 4 seconds (George's discovery, now automated), then switches back. No manual tab switching needed. Ads keep coming after reload? Switch to another tab for a few seconds, then switch back. Chrome throttles background tabs, which lets the ad state settle — George discovered this works every time. Incognito: see the Incognito section above. How It Works Ad detected → Capture timestamp → Reload page → Auto-seek to timestamp → Resume ↓ (if 3 reloads fail) Redirect to yout-ube.com (ad-free mirror, no looping) Two strategies Reload (primary) — reloads the page 1-3 times. YouTube re-evaluates ad serving on each reload; after 1-2 cycles the ad slot is empty and the video plays clean. Timestamp is preserved via &t=Xs URL param + JS seek. yout-ube.com redirect (fallback) — if reloads don't clear the ad after 3 attempts, redirects to yout-ube.com (an ad-free YouTube mirror). The URL includes &loop=0 to prevent the infinite replay issue that the mirror has by default. Detect — watches for .ad-showing class, skip buttons, and ad overlays (every 500ms + MutationObserver) Capture — grabs video.currentTime and saves it to sessionStorage Reload — location.replace() with &t=Xs in the URL Restore — YouTube auto-seeks to the timestamp; playback resumes Cooldown — 3-second guard prevents reload loops Features ✅ Zero ads — reloads until the ad is gone (usually 1-2 cycles) ✅ Timestamp preserved — never lose your place in the video ✅ Live streams — plain reload (no timestamp to preserve) ✅ Ad history database — every ad logged with advertiser, duration, skip text, video, and timestamp ✅ Export — JSON or CSV download of all collected ad data ✅ Popup viewer — click the extension icon to see stats, top advertisers, and full history ✅ No permissions abuse — only storage and tabs , only on YouTube domains Install Option A — Chrome / Brave / Edge / Opera (Load unpacked) Clone the repo: git clone https://github.com/antonpictures/youtube-punisher.git Open chrome://extensions Enable Developer mode (top right) Click Load unpacked → select the youtube-punisher folder Done — activates on all YouTube pages automatically. ✅ Tested Option B — Safari (experimental: AppleScript workaround) Safari blocks ad-hoc signed extensions from auto-injecting into YouTube. As a workaround, use the JS overlay + AppleScript watcher ( yt-ad-watch.sh ): In Safari, enable: Safari → Settings → Advanced → Show Develop menu in menu bar In Safari (on a YouTube page), run ./yt-ad-watch.sh in Terminal When an ad appears, the watcher detects it via MutationObserver (event-driven in the page), reloads with &t=Xs , and the MutationObserver re-detects on the next page load Note: This is best-effort. Chrome is fully reliable; Safari works but may need manual testing. Option C — Download zip Download the latest release from Releases Unzip and follow Option A steps 2–5 The Ad History Database Every ad YouTube serves you is recorded: Field What it captures Timestamp When the ad was detected Advertiser Company name from the ad overlay Video Title of the video you were watching Video time Your playback position before reload Ad duration Length of the ad Skip text "Skip Ad" button text (if available) Action Reloaded or skipped Export as JSON or CSV from the popup. Data stays local — nothing is sent anywhere. Why Reloads Work (and Why Nobody Thought of This) YouTube's ad system serves ads as part of the page load. When you reload, YouTube re-evaluates whether to serve an ad based on your session state. After 1-2 reloads, the ad slot is typically empty and the video plays directly. This is a client-side, zero-cost workaround — no filter lists, no network blocking, no detection by YouTube's anti-adblock system. The Scale Question If millions of users did this, each reload = a full page load = server request. YouTube would see a spike in page loads but a drop in ad impressions. It's not a DDoS (no amplification, no botnet), but it's a passive protest : every reload is a vote that says "I will not watch your ad." The ad revenue model breaks when reloads are cheaper than ad views. "Every reload is a vote: I will not watch your ad." — George Anton, creator Comparison with Other Tools Tool How it works Reloads? They don't conflict. title: Show HN: Fuck_data_brokers.py
abstract:
f*ck_data_brokers.py "Today was funny: I was dealing with some scumbag data broker this morning, trying to get a
good friend of mine's information deleted, and they WOULDN'T do it. No matter what I tried. I
felt so ugh! I just wanted to reach through the screen and punch them in the face. Well, Mr.
Data Broker, here's me reaching through the screen and punching you in the face. Enjoy
f*ck_data_brokers.py" I remove people's data from data brokers. It is one of my main part-time jobs, and it has been a wild ride. All I want to do is help people. In the world of AI that has become next to impossible. From where I sit, data brokers have ramped up production almost 1000x since GPT-4 came out. Every scraper got smarter, every profile got fatter, and every "people search" site got a hundred cousins. Then it hit me: I do not have a trillion dollars. By my rough estimate that is what it would cost in compute to clean up everyone's data for them, properly and automatically. I cannot do it for everyone. I am fed up with what everyone is put through. So here is my response: f*ck_data_brokers.py One Python file. No dependencies. Free. It runs on your computer, keeps your details on your computer, and makes data brokers delete you. Star this repository Every star is one more person these companies have to answer. The more stars, the sooner they learn their lesson. It costs you one click. It costs them a compliance department. The platinum option: let Agent Garrett do it This tool is free and always will be. It is also work: 600 companies, their excuses, their forms, their silence, and then next month they collect you again. Agent Garrett is the service I built to do all of it for you. Set it and forget it(you can do it for free with this tool if you cannot afford the subscription!). Persistence is guaranteed. Agent Garrett does not get bored, does not get tired and does not take "use our form" for an answer. A broker can stall a person. It cannot outlast a machine that never stops asking, and that is how removal happens: not with one letter, but with the one that never stops coming. Who these people are Data brokers are companies you have never heard of. They collect your name, your address, your phone number, your relatives and your habits, without asking. They sell all of it to anyone with a credit card. Then they write "we value your privacy" at the bottom of the page and expect you to keep a straight face. More than 600 of them signed a government registry admitting, in writing, that selling people is their business. That makes them very easy to find. What this does to them Gets the list of registered data brokers. All 600 and more. Writes each one a real legal deletion and opt-out letter in your name, quoting the law where you live. Sends the letters from your own free mailbox, or hands them to you ready to send. Reads what they write back and tells you which excuse it is and what to answer. Chases the ones that go quiet and tells you where to file a complaint about the ones that refuse. The tool is rude about data brokers. The letters are not. They are firm, correct and legal, because the goal is to leave a broker with nothing to hide behind. What you need Python 3.8 or newer. Check with python --version . If you do not have it, get it free from python.org . An email address. A free one is fine. That is all. No account, no subscription, no AI required. Use it without AI Download fuck_data_brokers.py , open a terminal in that folder, and run: python fuck_data_brokers.py You get a menu. Go down the list: Tell it who you are. Name, email, city, and where you live. No street address, no birthday, no ID. Brokers get the minimum. Get the list of data brokers. Write the deletion letters. It writes 20 at a time. Send them. See below. Come back when a broker answers, and pick A broker answered. What now? Paste the reply. It tells you what they are up to and writes your answer. Now and then, pick Chase the quiet ones . They will be quiet. They are counting on you giving up. Every menu item is also a command, if you prefer: python fuck_data_brokers.py --help . Sending the letters, for free You do not need to pay for an email service. Pick whichever is easier. The send page (no setup at all). After writing letters, the tool gives you a page called send.html . Open it in your browser. Each letter has a button that opens it in your email, already addressed and written. Press send. Next. If the button does not open your email, the page also has copy buttons for the address, the subject and the letter. When you are done, run python fuck_data_brokers.py sent all so the clock starts. Let the tool send them. Run python fuck_data_brokers.py send . It sends through your own mailbox and knows the settings for Gmail, Outlook, Yahoo and iCloud. It asks for an app password , which you create in your email account's security settings after turning on two-step sign-in. The password is used once and never saved. A separate free address just for this is a good idea. Their replies stay out of your real inbox. Put it on a schedule One command does everything that needs no decision from you: python fuck_data_brokers.py auto It refreshes the broker list, writes the next 20 letters, writes reminders for brokers that are late, and rebuilds your send page. Run it as often as you like; it never writes to the same broker twice. Add --send and it also sends, using the app password in the FDB_SMTP_PASS environment variable. Run it once a week and the whole list is covered in a few months without you thinking about it. On Linux or macOS, add a line to your crontab. On Windows, create a weekly task in Task Scheduler that runs the same command. 0 9 * * 1 python3 /path/to/fuck_data_brokers.py auto The one thing it cannot do for you is read your inbox. When a broker answers, paste the reply into reply . When a broker says "use our form" Some will not act on an email. They want you on their web form, behind a CAPTCHA, because a company that scrapes the internet with bots would like to be sure you are not a bot. Run python fuck_data_brokers.py forms . You get a page with a link to each broker's own form and copy buttons for exactly what to paste. You fill it in, you do the CAPTCHA, you press submit. Then tell the tool: python fuck_data_brokers.py sent req-1a2b3c4d . If a form demands a photo of your ID, close the tab. They sell personal data. They are not getting more of it from you. Then tell the tool, so the request does not die there: python fuck_data_brokers.py noid req-1a2b3c4d The request carries on in writing without the form. See What happens when I refuse to send ID? Use it with your AI The tool is also an MCP server, so an AI assistant that supports MCP can do the boring part for you. Add this to your AI app's MCP settings, with the real path to the file: { "mcpServers" : { "fuck_data_brokers" : { "command" : " python " , "args" : [ " /path/to/fuck_data_brokers.py " , " mcp " ] } }
} Then say: "Use fuck_data_brokers to get me deleted from data brokers." Your AI will ask who you are, fetch the broker list, write the letters, read the replies you give it, and write the answers. It is told to ask you before sending anything, never to invent your details, never to send an ID, and never to click a link from a broker. If your AI has a browser, it can fill in a broker's form while you watch. You still do the CAPTCHA and press submit yourself. They used AI to build a file on you. Use AI to make them delete it.
