title: NP_R ≠ PAR_R
abstract:
NP_R ≠ PAR_R: the permanent has no short real certificates Important The results in this repository grew out of a conversation between Samuel Everett and Claude Fable 5.2. The initial prompts were inspired by a separate discussion between Sam and Deven Mithal, the latter of whom suggested combining the latest VP-VNP results with some of Sam's private work in the area. This is a work in progress in both the development and dissemination of mathematical research with AI tools, and any feedback is appreciated. Claude Fable 5.2 found the proofs through the conversation with Sam, and then wrote the paper under his guidance.
That conversation started from initial ideas in a separate, earlier conversation Sam had with ChatGPT Astra 6.2, which proved $\mathrm{BIP} {\mathbb R}^{\times}\subsetneq\mathrm{PAR} {\mathbb R}^{\times}$ (Boolean-message interactive proofs against parallel polynomial time, in the real model with multiplication). The conversation with Claude Fable 5.2 extended that starting point to the further separations listed below.
All results are formalized in Lean 4 (see Lean formalization below), with the results cited from the literature as explicit hypotheses. The results have not been peer reviewed and should be read with that in mind. Results In the Blum–Shub–Smale (BSS) model, the graph {Y = per_m(X)} of the real permanent lies in parallel polynomial time PAR_ℝ and outside each of NP_ℝ and coNP_ℝ, the second existential level Σ₂ of the real polynomial hierarchy, constant-round Arthur–Merlin proofs with real messages, interactive proofs with Boolean messages (BIP_ℝ), and over the complex numbers outside NP_ℂ and coNP_ℂ. Each of these classes is therefore strictly contained in PAR_ℝ (respectively PAR_ℂ). Both closed thresholds, $Y \le \mathrm{per}_m(X)$ and $Y \ge \mathrm{per}_m(X)$ , also lie in PAR_ℝ and outside NP_ℝ, coNP_ℝ and Σ₂^ℝ. Negating one matrix row and the claimed value interchanges the thresholds. Their intersection is the graph. The separations use the superpolynomial lower bound for the border complexity of the permanent (Theorem 2.3 in the paper, cited from the Anthropic manuscript "VP ≠ VNP over every field" and its Lean formalization). Two families of results use no lower bound: the graph theorems: a polynomial of polynomial degree whose graph has short existential, universal or ∃∀ real certificates has small border complexity; AM_ℝ[O(1)] = NP_ℝ ⊊ AM_ℝ[poly]. Layout File Content main.tex Title, abstract, section includes macros.tex Notation refs.bib Bibliography sections/intro.tex Introduction and statements of the main theorems sections/prelim.tex Model, classes, border complexity, semialgebraic tools, cells sections/core.tex Derivatives of semialgebraic families, Newton iteration as a circuit, the local theorem sections/certificates.tex Existential certificates: graph theorem, thresholds, value functions sections/universal.tex Universal certificates and the complex field sections/second-level.tex An existential and a universal block sections/interaction.tex Boolean messages and constant-round Arthur–Merlin proofs sections/open.tex Open problems sections/lean.tex Appendix A: the Lean formalization, with the correspondence between results and Lean theorems lean/ The Lean 4 formalization (see lean/README.md ) Building latexmk -pdf main.tex Lean formalization The directory lean/ contains a formalization of the paper in Lean 4 (v4.36.0) with Mathlib (v4.36.0), about 36 000 lines. To check it: cd lean
lake exe cache get
lake build Every numbered lemma, proposition, theorem and corollary of §2–§7, Theorems A–F, and Remarks 4.3, 5.4 and 7.4(a) are stated and proved, with no sorry . #print axioms reports only propext , Classical.choice and Quot.sound for every result. The results that the paper cites are explicit hypotheses of the theorems that use them, not axioms: SAFacts — facts (S2)–(S8) on semialgebraic sets; PermLowerBound — Theorem 2.3, the border-complexity lower bound for the permanent; BurgisserThm — Theorem 2.5; EffectiveQE — effective quantifier elimination [BPR06]; CountingBound — the counting bound (C) of Lemma 7.7; ClassFacts — the known inclusions between complexity classes. In particular, every separation is conditional on PermLowerBound , exactly as in the paper. Fact (S1) holds by construction: semialgebraic sets are defined as first-order definable sets. Baur–Strassen, Ryser's formula, Hoeffding's inequality (from Mathlib) and the unrolling of machines into trees are proved. Appendix A of the paper ( sections/lean.tex ) and lean/README.md list the Lean name of each result, the modelling choices, and the few places where a formal proof differs from the text. lean/ClassSeparations/Pinned.lean restates the main statements verbatim and checks them against the proved theorems. Status The proofs have not been peer reviewed. The paper is mostly AI-written (see above). The results are formalized in Lean, conditional on the cited results listed above. The bibliographic data in refs.bib were checked against publisher and Crossref records. The numbered results cited from the Anthropic manuscript, Bürgisser (2004, 2026), Baartse–Meer, Baur–Strassen and Cucker et al. were confirmed in the sources. Still to be confirmed against the full texts: the attributions to Cucker (1992, 1993), Koiran (1994), Blum–Cucker–Shub–Smale, and the numbering in Basu–Pollack–Roy, which follows the second edition (2006).

title: Rvoip: VoIP stack in Rust
abstract:
rvoip A Rust library for building communications applications. SIP, RTP, WebRTC, QUIC/WebTransport/WebSocket conversations, Media over QUIC, and voice-AI agents share one call model, and the whole stack is in the box: no external SIP server, media server, or RTP engine to install and wire together. Five-minute start · For carriers · Which crate? · Pick a path · How it fits together · What ships · Interop evidence · Changes · Upgrading from 0.3 What rvoip is rvoip is a library, not a server you deploy next to your application. Signalling,
media, codecs, NAT traversal, security, and the conversation model are all
Rust crates in this workspace, so a call goes from your code to the wire without
a separately installed SIP proxy, media server, or RTP engine. The examples
below run on a laptop with nothing installed but Rust; the same crates carry
the release-gated interoperability evidence against Asterisk, FreeSWITCH,
Jambonz, Kamailio, and OpenSIPS. Carriers evaluating standards coverage,
performance, and reliability should start with For carriers . Historical performance: published 0.5.0 One AWS c8i.4xlarge (16 vCPU, 8 cores, Intel Xeon 6, 32 GiB) running a single
rvoip process, measured with the RFC 7501/7502 benchmark: Workload Max CPS CPS per vCPU Concurrent calls (10 s calls) p50 setup at 90% load p99 setup at 90% load SIP over TLS, signaling only 8,348 ~520 n/a 1 ms 6 ms SIP over UDP, signaling only 8,256 ~515 n/a 1 ms 6 ms TLS + SRTP (SDES), G.711, 10 s calls 1,124 ~70 ~11,200 1 ms 4 ms UDP + RTP, G.711, 10 s calls 1,204 ~75 ~12,000 n/m n/m At 2x capacity, rvoip keeps admitting calls at its max CPS, refuses the
excess with fast 503 responses, and recovers cleanly once the load drops. Max CPS (calls per second; RFC 7502's Session Establishment Rate) is the
highest rate with zero failed calls over a trial of at least 180 s and
50,000 call attempts. rvoip was measured as a terminating endpoint: it answers each call and echoes
its media. A relaying B2BUA or SBC handles two call legs per session. G.711 media is passed through; nothing is transcoded. Concurrent calls is the CPS times the 10 s call length, not a measured
maximum; long-call capacity, where most SBC datasheets quote their
concurrency, has not been measured yet. The server is a cloud VM, not an appliance. p50 and p99 setup are the RFC 6076 session request delay measured at 90% of
max CPS, recorded in whole milliseconds (so 1 ms means 1 ms or less);
n/m = not measured. The UDP + RTP max CPS was confirmed twice rather than three times. The release check also passed at 5% above the TLS and UDP signaling max CPS,
so those two figures may be slightly understated. Not yet measured: B2BUA/relay mode (two legs per call), registrations,
transcoding, WebRTC (DTLS-SRTP), and failover. Full method and per-trial data: RFC 7501/7502 benchmark report . Five-minute start 1. Add one dependency. [ dependencies ] rvoip-sip = " 0.5.1 " tokio = { version = " 1 " , features = [ " full " ] } Upgrading an existing application from 0.3? The 0.4 migration guide has before/after code for every
breaking change. 2. Make a call. Bob answers, Alice dials, Alice hangs up. Everything runs
on loopback, so this works on a laptop with no PBX, no account, and no network
setup. use std :: time :: Duration ; use rvoip_sip :: { Config , Endpoint , EndpointProfile } ; # [ tokio :: main ] async fn main ( ) -> rvoip_sip :: Result < ( ) > { let bob = tokio :: spawn ( async { let mut bob = Endpoint :: builder ( ) . name ( "bob" ) . profile ( EndpointProfile :: Custom ( Config :: local ( "bob" , 5071 ) ) ) . build ( ) . await ? ; let incoming = bob . wait_for_incoming ( ) . await ? ; let call = incoming . answer ( ) . await ? ; call . wait_for_end ( None ) . await ? ; bob . shutdown ( ) . await } ) ; tokio :: time :: sleep ( Duration :: from_millis ( 300 ) ) . await ; let alice = Endpoint :: builder ( ) . name ( "alice" ) . profile ( EndpointProfile :: Custom ( Config :: local ( "alice" , 5070 ) ) ) . build ( ) . await ? ; let call = alice . call_and_wait ( "sip:bob@127.0.0.1:5071" , Some ( Duration :: from_secs ( 10 ) ) ) . await ? ; call . hangup_and_wait ( Some ( Duration :: from_secs ( 5 ) ) ) . await ? ; alice . shutdown ( ) . await ? ; bob . await . unwrap ( ) } 3. Or run the same program from the checkout. git clone https://github.com/eisenzopf/rvoip.git && cd rvoip
cargo run -p rvoip-sip --example endpoint_local_call From here, examples/ walks forward one step at a time: real
microphone audio, registering to a PBX, hold/DTMF, transfers, SRTP and TLS, an
IVR, a B2BUA, then browser and voice-AI gateways. You need one crate The workspace contains 47 crates. You import one of them; it pulls in
everything it needs. The rest are internal layers you never name in your own Cargo.toml . You are building Depend on Enable A SIP phone, PBX, IVR, registrar, proxy, B2BUA, or trunk gateway rvoip-sip nothing extra One server that takes SIP and browser (WebRTC) callers and connects them rvoip features = ["app"] A SIP or WebRTC caller talking to a hosted voice agent (Vapi) rvoip features = ["app", "vapi"] Your own ASR / TTS / dialog pipeline, with recordings and signed vCons rvoip features = ["voip-3"] A native, mobile, or embedded client SDK rvoip-client pick transports Amazon Connect A2A callers bridged to an external agent rvoip-amazon-a2a — SIP calls delivered to Amazon Connect agents rvoip-amazon-connect — Media fan-out over Media over QUIC rvoip-moq — Two shortcuts: rvoip-sip is the release-gated product. If your application is
telephony, start and stay there. It is the only crate with a signed
interoperability attestation (see evidence ). rvoip is the facade. It re-exports rvoip-sip as rvoip::sip and adds
the shared Orchestrator plus optional transports and extensions behind
Cargo features. Its feature table and the deployment bundles ( bundle-sip-endpoint , bundle-carrier-sip , bundle-browser-gateway , bundle-ai-conversation , bundle-full-pure-rust , bundle-full-native ) are the only feature lists you
need. Deployment backends (Keycloak, LDAP, Redis, Postgres vCon storage, audit and
SIEM sinks, SAML, SCIM, WebAuthn, STIR/SHAKEN, IMS AKA) are separate rvoip-* extension crates you add only when you operate that backend. The extension catalog lists them. Pick your path For JavaScript UCTP control, see the experimental browser/Node WebSocket
client . It is available as source with TypeScript
declarations; the package is not yet published to npm. Application-profile
dispatch is a separate opt-in server extension that stock servers do not enable. Path 1 — SIP telephony ( rvoip-sip ) Four API surfaces, from simplest to most control. Most applications use the
first one. Surface Use it when Example Endpoint You want a softphone, an account that registers, or a scripted caller/callee 01-quickstart-p2p , 02-softphone-audio , 03-register-to-pbx StreamPeer You want a sequential "send, then wait for the matching event" client 04-call-control , 05-blind-transfer CallbackPeer You are writing a server that reacts to inbound calls (IVR, auto-attendant) 09-ivr-server UnifiedCoordinator + server::b2bua You need a PBX, registrar, proxy, or B2BUA with routing and media bridging 10-call-center-b2bua Register an account on a PBX and place a call through it: use std :: time :: Duration ; use rvoip_sip :: { Endpoint , EndpointProfile , Result } ; # async fn example ( ) -> Result < ( ) > { let mut endpoint = Endpoint :: builder ( ) . name ( "alice" ) . account ( "1001" ) . password ( "secret" ) . registrar ( "sips:pbx.example.com:5061" ) . profile ( EndpointProfile :: AsteriskTlsSrtpRegisteredFlow ) . build ( ) . await ? ; endpoint . register ( ) . await ? ; let call = endpoint . call_and_wait ( "1002" , Some ( Duration :: from_secs ( 30 ) ) ) . await ? ; call . send_dtmf ( '1' ) . await ? ; call . hangup_and_wait ( Some ( Duration :: from_secs ( 5 ) ) ) . await ? ; endpoint . shutdown ( ) . await ?

title: CTO of 'RansomwareHelp' indicted for wire fraud
abstract:
The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com , a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed. A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com. The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands. “Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.” But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the company’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media , but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company]. The indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors. The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260. The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260. Paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria . Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their company and client data. Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.” A portion of the proposal that RansomwareHelp sent to a victim accounting firm in March 2024. Click to enlarge. The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.” “Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed. Ihme said RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the company could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network. A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked. But Ihme said a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days. A screenshot of a 2024 conversation between Lockbit and RansomwareHelp, which was secretly negotiating with the extortion group. Click to enlarge. “The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme said. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.” Indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit quickly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and that the ransom demand would increase by $100,000 for every day they dithered further. The Lockbit representative starts raising the ransom demand after multiple negotiators begin interacting with the threat actors. Click to enlarge. In the end, the accounting firm took Ihme’s advice and went with a more established security firm that helped them negotiate a payment to Lockbit. “The victim told us, ‘If we don’t get this data back, our business is over’,” Ihme recalled. “They ended up paying half of what RansomwareHelp was going to charge them.” The chats show RansomwareHelp kept pestering Lockbit to negotiate a deal even after it was clear a new negotiator was engaging with the ransomware group on the victim’s behalf. “I tell you something, that person who is negotiating with you for the other chat is damaging the whole process,” RansomwareHelp wrote to Lockbit. “Please do not change the price. I am doing my best to achieve it.” Ihme said RansomwareHelp primarily targeted small to medium sized businesses that weren’t particularly tech-savvy, noting that many of the technical claims made on the company’s website and in their proposal are patently farcical. For example, the proposal sent to the accounting firm said it could break six types of encryption, and then proceeded to list a number of irrelevant password hashing algorithms like SHA-256. “If it were really true these guys could decrypt any ransomware out there, this guy would be a billionaire,” Ihme said. “They were going after people who don’t have any technical knowledge, are desperate, and don’t have anyone advising them about how any of this stuff works.” The case against Palacio marks the latest in a string of recent prosecutions by the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) targeting security firms alleged to have conspired with fraudsters to defraud clients. In early October, the government charged 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky , an executive at the Canadian cybersecurity firm Cybersteward.
